tamil:
ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும் சூதர்க்கும் உண்டாங்கொல்
நன்றெய்தி வாழ்வதோர் ஆறு.
transliteration:
Ondreydhi noorizhakkum soodharkkum undaangol
nandreydhi vaazhvadhor aaru.
current_meaning: Gamblers win one and lose a hundred. Can such people ever find a way to live a good life?
elementary: Imagine trading a hundred of your marbles for the chance to win one. You would soon have none left. Valluvar asks: if someone keeps doing that, how could life ever go well for them?
university: The couplet works through a stark ratio, ondreydhi noorizhakkum (ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும், 'gaining one, losing a hundred'), and then a rhetorical question ending in -kol (உண்டாங்கொல், 'will there be?'), which expects the answer no. Soodhar (சூதர்) means gamblers; aaru (ஆறு) is 'way, path', so nandreydhi vaazhvadhor aaru is 'a path of living that attains good'. The particle -um in soodharkkum ('even for gamblers') implies that other sinners may still find such a path, but gamblers, as a class, are shut out. Puliyur Kesikan on thirukkural.net softens the arithmetic to 'losing by hundreds out of the hope of gain', and Kalaignar reads it psychologically: a single win lures the player on into a hundred losses. Both base-text sites agree on the wording.

tamil:
உருளாயம் ஓவாது கூறின் பொருளாயம்
போஒய்ப் புறமே படும்.
transliteration:
Urulaayam oovaadhu koorin porulaayam
pooip purame padum.
current_meaning: If a person keeps betting on the rolling dice without stopping, their money and the income behind it will leave them and go to others.
elementary: A king who spends all day shouting bets at a dice board has no time left to look after his kingdom. Little by little, his treasure and his lands end up in other people's hands.
university: The couplet plays two compounds against each other: urulaayam (உருளாயம், 'gain from what rolls', i.e. the die, கவறு) and porulaayam (பொருளாயம், 'wealth and its revenue'). Oovaadhu koorin (ஓவாது கூறின்) means 'if one ceaselessly calls', which Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar take as calling out the stake, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as boasting of one's winnings. Pooip (போஒய், alapedai of போய்) purame padum says the wealth 'goes and lands outside', which Mu. Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss as 'reaches the enemies' (பகைவர்). Pope's English ('If prince unceasing speak of nought but play') and his prose gloss follow the traditional Parimelazhagar reading, which takes the subject to be a king, in keeping with the chapter's place in Porutpaal. The text is identical on both base sites.

tamil:
சிறுமை பலசெய்து சீரழிக்கும் சூதின்
வறுமை தருவதொன்று இல்.
transliteration:
Sirumai palaseydhu seerazhikkum soodhin
varumai tharuvadhondru il.
current_meaning: Nothing makes a person as poor as gambling. It brings many troubles and destroys a person's good name.
elementary: Some bad habits make you a little poorer. Gambling is the champion of them all: it takes your money, gets you into trouble, and makes people stop trusting you.
university: Sirumai pala seydhu (சிறுமை பல செய்து) means 'causing many miseries' (Mu. Varadarasanar: துன்பம் பலவற்றையும்), though sirumai literally means 'smallness, meanness' and can also suggest degradation. Seer (சீர்) here is renown or good standing, glossed as புகழ் by all four commentators. The superlative construction soodhin ... ondru il ('there is nothing like gambling') makes gambling the paramount cause of varumai (வறுமை, poverty). Textual note: both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print the verb as சீரழக்கும், but ytamizh's own transliteration ('seerazhikkum') and every gloss (கெடுக்கும், அழிக்கும்) support the standard சீரழிக்கும், so சீரழக்கும் looks like a shared typographical slip; this reading should be confirmed against a printed edition. Kesikan's gloss adds that gambling does this 'to those who love it' (தன்னை விரும்பியவருக்கு).

tamil:
கவறும் கழகமும் கையும் தருக்கி
இவறியார் இல்லாகி யார்.
transliteration:
Kavarum kazhagamum kaiyum tharukki
ivariyaar illaagi yaar.
current_meaning: People who were proud of the dice, the gambling hall and their own skill, and would not give them up, have ended up with nothing.
elementary: Some people are very proud of being good at a game, and they love the place where it is played. But if that game is gambling and they never stop, Valluvar says, they finish with empty pockets, as many before them did.
university: The first line names gambling's three parts: kavaru (கவறு, the dice), kazhagam (கழகம், the gaming hall) and kai (கை, the hand, meaning dexterity in throwing). Tharukki (தருக்கி) means 'taking pride in', and ivariyaar (இவறியார்) means 'those who clung to, would not let go'. Illaagiyaar (இல்லாகியார்) is past tense: 'became people who have nothing'. Pope's English brings this out ('the men in other days who came to nought'), and Solomon Pappaiah adds that this 'has happened before too' (முன்பும் உண்டு), so the couplet appeals to historical examples. Kesikan reads it as 'those once wealthy and now destitute', and Mu. Varadarasanar supplies the parenthetical 'even though they had every wealth'. Kesikan's text on thirukkural.net prints the dice as சுவறு, apparently a misprint for கவறு; the couplet itself is identical on both sites.

tamil:
அகடாரார் அல்லல் உழப்பர்சூ தென்னும்
முகடியான் மூடப்பட் டார்.
transliteration:
Agadaaraar allal uzhapparsoo thennum
mugadiyaan moodappat taar.
current_meaning: People covered over by the bad-luck goddess called gambling will never even fill their stomachs, and they will suffer many troubles.
elementary: Picture a big dark cloud named 'Bad Luck' that swallows people whole. Once it has you, you never get enough to eat and troubles keep coming. Valluvar says gambling is that cloud.
university: Mugadi (முகடி) is Misfortune personified, the goddess known in Tamil as Moodevi or Jyeshtha (மூதேவி), the inauspicious elder sister of Lakshmi. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss it as மூதேவி, and Pope's verse renders it 'Misfortune's other name'. Moodappattaar (மூடப்பட்டார்) means 'those covered or engulfed', which Mu. Varadarasanar renders as 'swallowed' (விழுங்கப்பட்டவர்). Agadaaraar (அகடாரார்) is 'those whose belly (அகடு) is never filled', and allal uzhappar means 'will toil in affliction'. Following Parimelazhagar's two-world reading, Kesikan and the Pope prose gloss take the second clause to mean suffering in the next world as well. Kesikan's text on thirukkural.net seems to drop the negation ('வயிறார உணவைப் பெறுவதுடன்'), which is likely a transcription slip. The couplet text matches on both sites.

tamil:
பழகிய செல்வமும் பண்பும் கெடுக்கும்
கழகத்துக் காலை புகின்.
transliteration:
Pazhagiya selvamum panbum kedukkum
kazhagaththuk kaalai pugin.
current_meaning: If a person spends their time in the gambling hall, it destroys both the riches they were born into and their good character.
elementary: Your grandparents may have saved a treasure for your family and taught you good manners. Valluvar says that hanging around a gambling house can waste both: the treasure is lost, and the good manners slowly disappear too.
university: Pazhagiya selvam (பழகிய செல்வம்) is 'long-familiar wealth', which all commentators take as ancestral or inherited property (Kalaignar: மூதாதையர் தேடிவைத்த சொத்து). Panbu (பண்பு) is good character or natural virtue. The second line contains an interpretive crux: kaalai (காலை) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Kesikan as kaalam, 'time' ('if one's time is passed in the gaming hall'), and Kesikan adds 'the time meant for doing good'. Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh reads it literally as 'morning' ('if one goes to the gaming hall in the morning'), the hour that should belong to work. Kazhagam (கழகம்) also appears in 935 as the gaming place. The couplet is identical on both sites.

tamil:
பொருள்கெடுத்துப் பொய்மேற் கொளீஇ அருள்கெடுத்து
அல்லல் உழப்பிக்கும் சூது.
transliteration:
Porulkeduththup poimer koleei arulkeduththu
allal uzhappikkum soodhu.
current_meaning: Gambling wastes your money, pushes you to lie, kills your kindness, and makes you suffer.
elementary: First gambling takes your money. Then you start fibbing to cover it up. Then you stop caring about other people. And at the end you are very unhappy. Valluvar lists these four steps like a staircase going down.
university: The couplet is a chain of four causative actions with gambling (soodhu, சூது) held back as the subject until the last word. Porul keduththu (பொருள்கெடுத்து) means 'ruining wealth'; poi mer koleei (பொய்மேற் கொளீஇ) means 'making one take up falsehood', where koleei is the causative alapedai form of kol ('take'); arul keduththu (அருள்கெடுத்து) means 'destroying compassion'. The last verb, uzhappikkum (உழப்பிக்கும், 'causes to toil in affliction'), is also causative. Arul, the compassion celebrated in Arattuppaal's chapter 25 (Aruludaimai), is the highest of the virtues lost. Kesikan follows the Parimelazhagar tradition in reading the misery as belonging to both worlds (இருமையும்), and the Pope prose gloss adds '(here and hereafter)'. Both base sites agree on the text.

tamil:
உடைசெல்வம் ஊண்ஒளி கல்விஎன்று ஐந்தும்
அடையாவாம் ஆயங் கொளின்.
transliteration:
Udaiselvam oon-oli kalvi-endru aindhum
adaiyaavaam aayang kolin.
current_meaning: If a person takes up gambling, these five things will never come to them: clothes, riches, food, fame and learning.
elementary: Think of five good things: clothes to wear, money, food, a good name, and learning. Valluvar says that if you make gambling your habit, all five walk away from you.
university: The couplet lists five goods: udai (உடை, clothing), selvam (செல்வம், wealth), oon (ஊண், food), oli (ஒளி, 'light', i.e. fame or renown) and kalvi (கல்வி, learning). Aayam (ஆயம்) here means gambling, and aayang kolin means 'if one takes it up'. Adaiyaavaam (அடையாவாம்) says these 'will not come to' him, so the stress is on goods that are never gained, not only goods lost. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kesikan list the five in reverse order (fame, learning, wealth, food, clothing), presumably following Parimelazhagar's ranking from highest to lowest, while Pope keeps the Kural's order. Kesikan adds 'even if one does it thinking it mere sport' (வேடிக்கை), and Sivayogi Sivakumar takes oli as 'self-knowledge'. The text is the same on both sites.

tamil:
இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல் துன்பம்
உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர்.
transliteration:
Izhaththoruum kaadhalikkum soodhepol thunbam
uzhaththoruum kaadhatru uyir.
current_meaning: The more a gambler loses, the more they love gambling. In the same way, the more a soul suffers, the more it loves living in the body.
elementary: Have you ever lost a game and immediately shouted, 'One more try!'? The more you lose, the more you want to play. Valluvar says life is like that too: even when it hurts, we hold on to it more tightly.
university: The closing couplet turns a psychological observation about gambling into a general statement about existence. Izhaththoruum (இழத்தொறூஉம்) and uzhaththoruum (உழத்தொறூஉம்), both with alapedai, mean 'every time one loses' and 'every time one suffers', placing loss and pain in parallel. Kaadhalikkum (காதலிக்கும், 'comes to love') and kaadhatru (காதற்று) carry the comparison. Most commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Kesikan, Pope) read kaadhatru as kaadhal + atru, 'has love, is fond': the soul (uyir) loves the body more as it suffers, just as the gambler loves gambling more as he loses. Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh instead splits it as kaadhal + atru 'without love', giving the opposite sense that the soul does not love suffering, and adds that gambling can lead to despair. Pappaiah reverses which half is the comparison. The text is identical on both sites.

tamil:
மிகினும் குறையினும் நோய்செய்யும் நூலோர்
வளிமுதலா எண்ணிய மூன்று.
transliteration:
Miginum kuraiyinum noiseyyum noolor
valimudhalaa enniya moondru.
current_meaning: The three forces in the body that medical books name, starting with wind, cause sickness when there is too much or too little of them.
elementary: Think of a bicycle tyre: pump in too much air and it bursts, let out too much and it goes flat. Valluvar says the body has three such forces inside it, and it stays healthy only when each one is just right.
university: The chapter opens with theory before practice: noolor (நூலோர், 'the authors of the treatises') are the medical writers, and vali mudhalaa enniya moondru (வளிமுதலா எண்ணிய மூன்று, 'the three reckoned with wind first') are the three humours that Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss as vaatham, piththam and silethumam (வாதம், பித்தம், சிலேத்துமம்), i.e. the vata-pitta-kapha triad of Ayurveda and Siddha medicine. The decisive words are miginum kuraiyinum (மிகினும் குறையினும், 'whether in excess or in deficiency'): illness is defined not as an invading thing but as loss of proportion. Following Parimelazhagar, Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan add that the humours are disturbed through a person's food and activity (உணவும் செயல்களும்), which is why the following couplets turn at once to eating. The chapter closes the Natpiyal section of Porutpaal in the traditional arrangement, a placement commentators explain by treating bodily health as the last of the things a ruler and householder must secure. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மருந்தென வேண்டாவாம் யாக்கைக்கு அருந்தியது
அற்றது போற்றி உணின்.
transliteration:
Marundhena vendaavaam yaakkaikku arundhiyadhu
atradhu potri unin.
current_meaning: The body needs no medicine if a person eats only after making sure the last meal has been fully digested.
elementary: You would not pour more water into a glass that is still full; it would spill everywhere. Valluvar says the stomach is like that glass: wait until it has finished the last meal before you fill it again, and you will hardly ever need a doctor.
university: The couplet makes a bold claim, that medicine (marundhu, மருந்து) becomes unnecessary (vendaavaam, வேண்டாவாம்) for the body (yaakkai, யாக்கை), on one condition: arundhiyadhu atradhu potri unin (அருந்தியது அற்றது போற்றி உணின்), 'if one eats after carefully confirming that what was taken has been digested'. Atradhu (அற்றது, literally 'that which has ceased') is the technical verb for complete digestion that recurs in 943 and 944. Potri (போற்றி) means not 'praising' here but 'observing with care'; Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as examining the state of digestion, and Kalaignar as allowing the proper interval between meals. Parimelazhagar's tradition reads the hyperbole as a statement of priority: prevention through regimen ranks above cure. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அற்றால் அறவறிந்து உண்க அஃதுடம்பு
பெற்றான் நெடிதுய்க்கும் ஆறு.
transliteration:
Atraal aravarindhu unga ahdhudambu
petraan nedidhuykkum aaru.
current_meaning: After your last meal is digested, eat the right amount. That is how a person who has a body can keep it going for a long time.
elementary: A car runs far if you fill the tank properly and do not overflow it. Valluvar says your body is a gift you have been given, and eating the right amount at the right time is how you make it last a long, long time.
university: Atraal (அற்றால், 'when it has been digested') picks up the condition of 942, and adds aravarindhu (அறவறிந்து, அற + அறிந்து): Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read it as knowing the needed quantity, Puliyur Kesikan simply as eating in measure. The second line names the payoff: udambu petraan (உடம்பு பெற்றான், 'he who has obtained a body') can nedidhu uykkum (நெடிது உய்க்கும், 'carry it on long'). Kesikan glosses the body as 'this human frame so hard to obtain' (பெறுவதற்கரியதான இந்த மானிட யாக்கை), an Indian commonplace that human birth is rare and should not be wasted through gluttony. Parimelazhagar's line of interpretation thus links diet to longevity, not merely to comfort. Some editions print the first line as அற்றால் அளவறிந்து; ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net both read அறவறிந்து.

tamil:
அற்றது அறிந்து கடைப்பிடித்து மாறல்ல
துய்க்க துவரப் பசித்து.
transliteration:
Atradhu arindhu kadaippidiththu maaralla
thuykka thuvarap pasiththu.
current_meaning: Make sure your last meal is digested. Then stick to foods that suit your body, and eat them only when you are really hungry.
elementary: A plant needs water, but only when its soil has dried, and only clean water, not juice or soda. Valluvar says eat when you are really hungry, and choose the food that suits your body.
university: The couplet adds two refinements to the rule of digestion. Maaralla (மாறல்ல, 'things that are not contrary') are foods that do not disagree with one's constitution; Pappaiah extends this to foods unsuited to the body and to the season (உடம்பிற்கும் காலத்திற்கும் ஒவ்வாத). Kadaippidiththu (கடைப்பிடித்து) means holding firmly to such foods as a fixed practice. Thuvarap pasiththu (துவரப் பசித்து), 'being thoroughly hungry', makes real hunger, not appetite or habit, the signal to eat. Pope's translation renders the sense as 'when hunger prompteth thee, with constant care, the viands choose that well agree'. The idea of wholesome and unwholesome food relative to the person (Sanskrit satmya) is shared with Ayurveda, and the Parimelazhagar tradition reads the couplet as practical dietetics. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மாறுபாடு இல்லாத உண்டி மறுத்துண்ணின்
ஊறுபாடு இல்லை உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Maarupaadu illaadha undi maruththunnin
oorupaadu illai uyirkku.
current_meaning: If you eat food that suits your body and stop before you eat too much, no harm will come to your life.
elementary: Even your favourite ice cream will give you a tummy ache if you eat the whole tub. Valluvar says that even good food must be eaten with a 'no, that's enough' at the right moment.
university: Maarupaadu illaadha undi (மாறுபாடு இல்லாத உண்டி) is food that does not clash with the body, the same category as maaralla in 944. The key word is maruththu (மறுத்து, 'refusing'): Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as refusing more once the measure is reached, and Kesikan as eating not as the mind desires but only as much as causes no illness. Solomon Pappaiah takes a different line, reading maruththu as rejecting unsuitable foods, so that the couplet becomes about selection rather than quantity; this is a genuine interpretive divergence. Oorupaadu (ஊறுபாடு) is injury or harm, and uyirkku (உயிர்க்கு) 'to life' or 'to the soul dwelling in the body'. Parimelazhagar's reading, followed by most modern commentators, stresses restraint even with good food. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இழிவறிந்து உண்பான்கண் இன்பம்போல் நிற்கும்
கழிபேர் இரையான்கண் நோய்.
transliteration:
Izhivarindhu unbaankan inbampol nirkum
kazhiper iraiyaankan noi.
current_meaning: Good health stays with a person who knows to eat a little less. In the same way, sickness stays with a person who eats far too much.
elementary: Two friends go to a party. One eats until he is nicely full and goes home happy. The other stuffs himself and spends the night with a stomach ache. Valluvar says that is how it goes every time.
university: The couplet is a balanced antithesis. Izhivu (இழிவு) here means 'lessness': Varadarasanar glosses izhivarindhu unbaan as one who knows what the lesser measure is, and Kesikan as one who eats a little below the full measure; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it more morally as one who knows that taking more than needed is base, exploiting the word's other sense of 'meanness'. Inbam (இன்பம்) is well-being or pleasure, which nirkum (நிற்கும், 'stays, abides'). Kazhiper iraiyaan (கழிபேர் இரையான்) is a striking phrase: irai (இரை) is the word for an animal's prey or fodder, so the glutton is pictured as a beast gulping feed, and kazhiper (கழிபேர்) intensifies it to 'exceedingly great'. Disease abides with him as surely as health with the moderate eater. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தீயள வன்றித் தெரியான் பெரிதுண்ணின்
நோயள வின்றிப் படும்.
transliteration:
Theeyala vandrith theriyaan peridhunnin
noyala vindrip padum.
current_meaning: A person who carelessly eats far more than their stomach's fire (the body's power to digest) can handle will get sicknesses without end.
elementary: A small campfire can cook a small pot. If you pile a whole tree on it, the fire chokes and smoke goes everywhere. Valluvar says your tummy has a little fire too, and if you overload it, troubles pile up.
university: The couplet turns on a wordplay of measure: thee alavu (தீ அளவு, 'the measure of the fire') against noi alavu indri (நோய் அளவின்றி, 'diseases without measure'). The fire is the pasi-thee (பசித்தீ), the 'fire of hunger' or digestive fire, as Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss it; it corresponds to the Ayurvedic jatharagni, whose strength determines how much food can be digested. Theriyaan (தெரியான்) is 'one who does not discern', and Kesikan adds that he ignores both the time and the quantity. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads thee alavu instead as an analogy to one who does not know how to use fire in measure, a minority reading. Parimelazhagar's tradition takes the metaphor medically, so that the couplet states a law: exceed the fire's measure and illness exceeds all measure. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நோய்நாடி நோய்முதல் நாடி அதுதணிக்கும்
வாய்நாடி வாய்ப்பச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Noinaadi noimudhal naadi adhuthanikkum
vaainaadi vaaippach cheyal.
current_meaning: Find out what the sickness is, find its cause, find the way to ease it, and then treat it in the right way.
elementary: When your bike makes a funny noise, a good mechanic first finds which part is wrong, then why it broke, then how to fix it, and only then gets out the tools. Valluvar says a good doctor does the same with a sick person.
university: The most quoted couplet of the chapter is built on a threefold naadi (நாடி, 'having examined'): the disease (noi), its root or first cause (noi mudhal, நோய் முதல்), and the means (vaai, வாய்) that will abate it (thanikkum, தணிக்கும்). Only then comes vaaippach cheyal (வாய்ப்பச் செயல்), 'act fittingly': Kesikan reads it as treating without error in procedure, Varadarasanar as in a way suited to the body. Commentators note the sequence of diagnosis, aetiology and therapy as a complete clinical method; Kalaignar adds that it applies to the ills of society as well as of the body. The repetition of naadi and of vaai/vaaippa gives the line a deliberate, step-by-step rhythm. The couplet appears in the sung version of the chapter by P. A. Muthukrishnan quoted on thirukkural.net. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உற்றான் அளவும் பிணியளவும் காலமும்
கற்றான் கருதிச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Utraan alavum piniyalavum kaalamum
katraan karudhich cheyal.
current_meaning: A trained doctor should think about the patient, how serious the sickness is, and the time or season before treating it.
elementary: A baby and a grown-up with the same cold do not get the same dose of medicine. Valluvar says a good doctor thinks about who is sick, how sick they are, and what time it is before deciding what to do.
university: Three measures must be weighed: utraan alavu (உற்றான் அளவு), the measure of the one afflicted, which Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss as age and the like, and Kesikan as the patient's strength; pini alavu (பிணியளவு), the extent and nature of the disease; and kaalam (காலம்), which Sivayogi Sivakumar reads as the climate of the season, Kalaignar as the right time for treatment, and Pappaiah as both the duration of the illness and the time needed to cure it. The agent is katraan (கற்றான்), 'the one who has learned', i.e. the physician trained in the medical texts, and karudhi (கருதி) means 'having deliberated'. The couplet thus individualises treatment, echoing Ayurveda's attention to the patient's constitution and to season (ritu). Pope renders it 'the habitudes of patient and disease, the crises of the ill these must the learned leech think over well'. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உற்றவன் தீர்ப்பான் மருந்துழைச் செல்வானென்று
அப்பால் நாற்கூற்றே மருந்து.
transliteration:
Utravan theerppaan marundhuzhaich chelvaanendru
appaal naarkootre marundhu.
current_meaning: Medicine has four parts: the patient, the doctor who cures, the medicine, and the helper who stays close to give it.
elementary: Getting better is like a team game. The sick person must follow the plan, the doctor must know what to do, the medicine must be good, and someone like a parent or nurse must help every day. If one player is missing, the team struggles.
university: The chapter ends by defining medicine as naarkootru (நாற்கூற்று, 'fourfold'): utravan (உற்றவன், the one afflicted), theerppaan (தீர்ப்பான், the one who cures), marundhu (மருந்து, the remedy), and marundhuzhaich chelvaan (மருந்துழைச் செல்வான், literally 'he who goes near the medicine'). This last term divides the commentators: Varadarasanar reads it as the one who gives the medicine from close by, Kalaignar as the attendant at the bedside, Pappaiah and Kesikan as the preparer or compounder, and Pope's explanation as the compounder. The words appaal (அப்பால், 'that domain') and the closing marundhu frame the whole. Pope's gloss, following Parimelazhagar, adds that each of the four has four qualities in turn, sixteen in all. The fourfold scheme closely matches the Charaka Samhita's 'four feet' of therapy (physician, drug, attendant, patient), which is strong evidence that Valluvar knew the classical medical tradition. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இற்பிறந்தார் கண்அல்லது இல்லை இயல்பாகச்
செப்பமும் நாணும் ஒருங்கு.
transliteration:
Irpirandhaar kan alladhu illai iyalpaagach
cheppamum naanum orungu.
current_meaning: Doing what is right and feeling ashamed of wrong, found together as a natural habit, are seen only in people born into a good family.
elementary: Some children say sorry and play fair without anyone telling them, because they have seen it at home every day. Valluvar says that fairness and feeling bad about doing wrong come most naturally to people who grew up in a good home.
university: The chapter opens the Kudiyiyal (குடியியல், the section on the citizen and his family) of Porutpal, and its first couplet sets the theme: kudimai (குடிமை) is the character that a good lineage (இல், 'house', hence family) is expected to carry. Cheppam (செப்பம்) is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar as நடுவு நிலைமை, 'impartiality, rectitude', and by Solomon Pappaiah as purity of mind, word and deed; naanum (நாணும்) is shame or modesty, the recoil from what is unworthy. The force lies in iyalpaaga (இயல்பாக, 'by nature') and orungu (ஒருங்கு, 'together'): others may show one quality by effort, but the high-born show both effortlessly. Kalaignar's modern gloss reverses the direction, saying that only those who possess these qualities may be counted high-born, an egalitarian reading of a couplet that the medieval commentarial tradition read more literally. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஒழுக்கமும் வாய்மையும் நாணும்இம் மூன்றும்
இழுக்கார் குடிப்பிறந் தார்.
transliteration:
Ozhukkamum vaaymaiyum naanum im moondrum
izhukkaar kudippirandhaar.
current_meaning: People born into a good family never slip from these three things: good behaviour, telling the truth, and a sense of shame about doing wrong.
elementary: Think of a three-legged stool: good behaviour, telling the truth, and feeling bad about doing wrong. If one leg breaks, the stool falls. Valluvar says people from a good family keep all three legs strong.
university: The couplet names a triad: ozhukkam (ஒழுக்கம், right conduct, the subject of chapter 14), vaaymai (வாய்மை, truthfulness, chapter 30) and naan (நாண், shame, which will receive its own chapter, 102). The verb izhukkaar (இழுக்கார்) means 'they do not slip or lapse', so the claim is about steadiness over a lifetime, not occasional virtue. Mu. Varadarasanar adds that the well-born live in the right path 'by nature' (இயல்பாகவே), linking this couplet to the iyalpaaga of 951, while Kalaignar again turns it into a definition: only those who never lapse in these three are to be counted high-born, and he glosses naan as maanam (மானம், honour). The word division நாணும்இம் மூன்றும் (naanum im moondrum, 'shame, these three') appears in both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நகைஈகை இன்சொல் இகழாமை நான்கும்
வகையென்ப வாய்மைக் குடிக்கு.
transliteration:
Nagai eegai insol igazhaamai naangum
vagaiyenba vaaymaik kudikku.
current_meaning: A smiling face, giving to others, kind words, and never looking down on anyone: the wise say these four are the marks of a truly good family.
elementary: When a friend visits, a kind family smiles, shares their snacks, speaks nicely and never makes fun of anyone. Valluvar says those four habits show you what a truly good family looks like.
university: The couplet lists four marks (naangum, நான்கும்): nagai (நகை, a smiling or cheerful countenance), eegai (ஈகை, giving, the subject of chapter 23), insol (இன்சொல், pleasant speech, chapter 10) and igazhaamai (இகழாமை, not scorning or belittling). Vaaymaik kudi (வாய்மைக் குடி) means a family that is genuinely, not nominally, noble; Puliyur Kesikan reads it as a lineage that never changes its character, and he applies the four marks especially to one's conduct towards the poor. Vagai (வகை) is 'kind' or 'proper quality', and enba (என்ப, 'they say') marks the list as received wisdom. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அடுக்கிய கோடி பெறினும் குடிப்பிறந்தார்
குன்றுவ செய்தல் இலர்.
transliteration:
Adukkiya kodi perinum kudippirandhaar
kundruva seydhal ilar.
current_meaning: Even if they could get crores upon crores (huge piles of money), people from good families will not do anything that brings their family down.
elementary: Imagine someone offers you a giant pile of money if you will just cheat once. A person from a good family says no, because no pile of money is worth losing their good name.
university: Adukkiya kodi (அடுக்கிய கோடி) is 'crores stacked one upon another', hyperbole for limitless wealth, and perinum (பெறினும், 'even if they obtain') concedes the strongest temptation. Kundruva (குன்றுவ) are acts that diminish, literally 'that make small', and the commentators unanimously take the diminished thing to be the family's honour: Mu. Varadarasanar speaks of faults that would lower the family's distinction, and Kalaignar of deeds that would spoil that excellence. The couplet thus sets the chapter's characteristic contrast between wealth (Porul) and the inherited good name that the section on family (Kudiyiyal) values above it. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வழங்குவ துள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும் பழங்குடி
பண்பில் தலைப்பிரிதல் இன்று.
transliteration:
Vazhanguvadhu ulveezhndhak kannum pazhangudi
panbil thalaippiridhal indru.
current_meaning: Even when they have less and less to give away, people from old, good families never lose their giving nature.
elementary: A grandmother who used to cook big meals for everyone now has only a little rice, but she still shares it with a hungry neighbour. Valluvar says that is how people from a good old family act: they keep giving even when they have little.
university: Vazhanguvadhu (வழங்குவது) is 'that which is given', and ulveezhndha (உள்வீழ்ந்த) means 'fallen inward, shrunk', so the opening line pictures the family's power of giving contracting through poverty; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as the capacity to give having dwindled through want. Pazhangudi (பழங்குடி) is 'the ancient family', the old line whose character is long established, and thalaippiridhal (தலைப்பிரிதல்) means 'to separate from', here from their panbu (பண்பு, nature, especially the generous disposition). Sivayogi Sivakumar and Solomon Pappaiah both specify that it is the giving nature that endures, while Kalaignar explicitly names poverty as the blow. Both sites print the words as வழங்குவ துள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும், a traditional metrical division of வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும்.

tamil:
சலம்பற்றிச் சால்பில செய்யார்மா சற்ற
குலம்பற்றி வாழ்தும்என் பார்.
transliteration:
Salampatrich chaalbila seyyaar maasatra
kulampatri vaazhdhum enbaar.
current_meaning: People who decide to live true to their spotless family name will never use tricks or do anything shameful.
elementary: If your family has always been known for honesty, you think, 'I will not be the one who spoils our name.' So you do not cheat, even when it would be easy.
university: Salam (சலம்) means deceit or crookedness, which Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar render as vanchanai (வஞ்சனை); chaalbila (சால்பில) are acts lacking saalbu (சால்பு, worthiness, nobility of character, the subject of chapter 99). Maasatra kulam (மாசற்ற குலம்) is 'a family free of stain', and vaazhdhum enbaar (வாழ்தும் என்பார்) are 'those who say, we shall live (by it)', so the couplet describes a conscious resolve to keep faith with an unblemished line. Solomon Pappaiah adds 'even when poverty comes', reading the couplet as continuing the thought of 955 that hardship tests the well-born. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, both dividing the line as மா சற்ற / மாசற்ற across the metrical break.

tamil:
குடிப்பிறந்தார் கண்விளங்கும் குற்றம் விசும்பின்
மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து.
transliteration:
Kudippirandhaar kan vilangum kutram visumbin
madhikkan maruppol uyarndhu.
current_meaning: A fault in someone from a good family stands out for everyone to see, like the dark spot on the moon high in the sky.
elementary: A tiny ink spot on a dirty shirt is hard to see, but the same spot on a bright white shirt is easy to notice. Valluvar says that a small mistake by someone from a respected family shows up just like that spot.
university: The simile is visumbin madhikkan maru (விசும்பின் மதிக்கண் மறு), 'the blemish on the moon in the sky'; maru (மறு) is a spot or stain, which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses as kalangam (களங்கம்). Uyarndhu (உயர்ந்து, 'being high, raised up') does double work: the moon is high in the sky, and the well-born are high in society, so their flaws are exposed to everyone. Puliyur Kesikan adds that the fault may be small in size yet known to the whole world, and Kalaignar notes that it shows 'without any concealment'. Sivayogi Sivakumar's gloss reads the image as the full moon itself, but the standard commentators understand the dark mark on its face. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நலத்தின்கண் நாரின்மை தோன்றின் அவனைக்
குலத்தின்கண் ஐயப் படும்.
transliteration:
Nalaththinkan naarinmai thondrin avanaik
kulaththinkan aiyap padum.
current_meaning: If someone who seems good shows a lack of love and kindness, people will start to doubt which family they really come from.
elementary: If a boy from a famously kind family is mean to a puppy, people say, 'Is he really from that kind family?' Valluvar says that being unkind makes others wonder where you came from.
university: Naar (நார்) is literally 'fibre', the tough strand that binds, and by extension affection or love; naarinmai (நாரின்மை) is the want of it, which Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan gloss as anbu-inmai or arul-inmai, lack of love or compassion. The opening word nalam (நலம்) is read in several ways: Mu. Varadarasanar takes it as one's good qualities, Puliyur Kesikan as the family's distinction, and Kalaignar as beauty and renown. Aiyap padum (ஐயப் படும், 'will be doubted') makes the striking claim that conduct can call ancestry itself into question, which is the hinge between this chapter's praise of lineage and the ethical reading that says character, not birth, is the real proof. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை கால்காட்டும் காட்டும்
குலத்தில் பிறந்தார்வாய்ச் சொல்.
transliteration:
Nilaththil kidandhamai kaal kaattum kaattum
kulaththil pirandhaarvaaich chol.
current_meaning: A sprout shows what kind of soil it grew in. In the same way, a person's words show what kind of family they come from.
elementary: A healthy green plant tells you the soil is good. In the same way, when someone speaks kindly and wisely, you can tell they grew up in a good home.
university: The image is agricultural: kaal (கால்) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan as mulai (முளை), the sprout or shoot, which reveals (kaattum, காட்டும்) what lay hidden in the soil (nilaththil kidandhamai, நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை). Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar widen it to the crop that grows there. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads kaal in its common sense of 'foot', so that the soil clinging to one's feet shows where one has walked; this is a minority reading that the standard commentators do not follow. The repetition kaattum kaattum (காட்டும் காட்டும்) closes the simile and opens its application: so too the speech (vaaich chol, வாய்ச்சொல்) of those born in a family reveals that family. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நலம்வேண்டின் நாணுடைமை வேண்டும் குலம்வேண்டின்
வேண்டுக யார்க்கும் பணிவு.
transliteration:
Nalamvendin naanudaimai vendum kulamvendin
venduga yaarkkum panivu.
current_meaning: If you want to be good, you must have a sense of shame about doing wrong. If you want your family to be respected, be modest and polite toward everyone.
elementary: Kids who say 'I'm the best!' all the time do not get respect. Kids who are polite to everyone, even the youngest, do. Valluvar says that if you want your family to be respected, be humble with everyone.
university: The closing couplet turns the chapter from description to instruction with a double condition built on the verb vendu (வேண்டு, 'to want, to require'): nalam vendin (நலம் வேண்டின், 'if you want good') requires naanudaimai (நாணுடைமை, the possession of shame), and kulam vendin (குலம் வேண்டின், 'if you want family standing') requires panivu (பணிவு, humility) towards yaarkkum (யார்க்கும், everyone). Puliyur Kesikan specifies shame at blame (பழிக்கு நாணம்), and Kalaignar adds 'without arrogance' (ஆணவமின்றி). The effect is to make lineage something earned and maintained by humility rather than simply inherited, which ties the chapter's ending back to the 'by nature' of 951. Naanudaimai is also the title of chapter 102, and the two chapters are often read together. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இன்றி அமையாச் சிறப்பின ஆயினும்
குன்ற வருப விடல்.
transliteration:
Indri amaiyaach chirappina aayinum
Kundra varupa vidal.
current_meaning: Even if something seems so important that you cannot live without it, give it up if doing it would lower your self-respect.
elementary: Imagine you could win the biggest prize at school, but only by copying someone else's answers. The prize feels like something you cannot live without, but this kural says: if getting it makes you smaller inside, walk away from it.
university: The chapter on maanam (மானம், honour, self-respect) follows Kudimai (Nobility of Family) and is read in the Parimelazhagar tradition as the quality of never sinking below one's station. The opening couplet sets the bar at its highest: indri amaiyaa (இன்றி அமையா, 'that without which one cannot exist') describes acts that seem indispensable, and kundra varupa (குன்ற வருப) are acts that bring about a 'lowering' (kundru, to diminish), which must be let go (vidal, விடல்). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan both gloss the lowering as a fall in kudi-p-perumai (the honour of one's lineage), tying the chapter to the preceding one; Kalaignar generalises it to one's own dignity. The Pope translation quoted on ytamizh.com renders it 'Reject each act that may thine honour's clearness stain.' The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
சீரினும் சீரல்ல செய்யாரே சீரொடு
பேராண்மை வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Seerinum seeralla seyyaare seerodu
Peraanmai vendu pavar.
current_meaning: People who want both a good name and true greatness will not do anything shameful, even if it would make them famous.
elementary: Some people will do anything to become famous, even mean or silly things. This kural says that people who want to be both well-known and truly good will never do something shameful just to get noticed.
university: The couplet plays on seer (சீர், renown, excellence): seerinum (சீரினும், 'even for renown') and seeralla (சீரல்ல, 'what is not excellent', unworthy deeds). Those who desire seerodu peraanmai (சீரொடு பேராண்மை), renown together with great 'manliness' or nobility of spirit, do not do such things. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses peraanmai as பெரிய ஆண்மை and the unworthy acts as those unfit for kudi-p-perumai (family honour); Kalaignar reads it as a heroic life that will not chase fame by acts contrary to self-respect. The point sharpens the previous kural: not only necessity but even fame itself cannot justify a lowering act. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல் சிறிய
சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு.
transliteration:
Perukkaththu vendum panidhal siriya
Surukkaththu vendum uyarvu.
current_meaning: When you have plenty, be modest and gentle. When you have very little, hold your head high.
elementary: When you win a game, it is good to be kind and not show off. When you lose, it is good to stand tall and not beg or sulk. This kural says to bow a little in good times and stand straight in hard times.
university: A perfectly balanced antithesis: perukkam (பெருக்கம், increase, prosperity) is set against surukkam (சுருக்கம், contraction, want), and panidhal (பணிதல், bending, humility) against uyarvu (உயர்வு, height, unbending dignity). Siriya (சிறிய, 'small') intensifies the second half: in a narrow, reduced state. Mu. Varadarasanar reads uyarvu as 'height that does not bow' (பணியாத உயர்வு), and Solomon Pappaiah as not stooping to others in poverty. Maanam here is not pride but a discipline that runs against circumstance: humble when one could afford arrogance, upright when one is tempted to grovel. Pope's version on ytamizh.com: 'Bow down thy soul, with increase blest, in happy hour; / Lift up thy heart, when stript of all by fortune's power.' Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
தலையின் இழிந்த மயிரனையர் மாந்தர்
நிலையின் இழிந்தக் கடை.
transliteration:
Thalaiyin izhindha mayiranaiyar maandhar
Nilaiyin izhindhak kadai.
current_meaning: When people fall from their honourable place, they become like hair that has fallen from the head: worth nothing.
elementary: Hair on your head is combed and cared for. But once a hair falls on the floor, nobody wants it. This kural says a person who drops their good behaviour and self-respect loses the respect others gave them, just like that fallen hair.
university: The simile works through a single verb, izhi (இழி, to descend, fall, be debased), used twice: hair izhindha from the head (fallen) and people izhindha from their nilai (நிலை, station, standing). On the head, hair is an ornament; once fallen it is swept away. Mu. Varadarasanar reads thalai as both 'head' and 'high place' (தலைமை), so the image doubles as falling from leadership. The Parimelazhagar tradition places this after 963 to show what happens when the discipline of maanam fails. Kalaignar applies it to someone who held a high place in people's hearts. Pope: 'Like hairs from off the head that fall to earth, / When fall'n from high estate are men of noble birth.' Both online texts read இழிந்தக் கடை.

tamil:
குன்றின் அனையாரும் குன்றுவர் குன்றுவ
குன்றி அனைய செயின்.
transliteration:
Kundrin anaiyaarum kundruvar kundruva
Kundri anaiya seyin.
current_meaning: Even people as great as a mountain become small if they do something low, even something as tiny as a kunri seed (a small red bean).
elementary: A big, beautiful glass of milk can be spoiled by one tiny drop of ink. This kural says even a very great person can lose respect by doing one small mean thing.
university: A celebrated piece of wordplay on the root kundru (குன்று): kundru as noun means 'hill' (kundrin anaiyaar, those like a hill), as verb 'to diminish' (kundruvar, they will be lowered), kundruva are 'diminishing' (debasing) acts, and kundri (குன்றி) is the kunrimani, the small red-and-black seed of Abrus precatorius used as a jeweller's weight. The contrast of hill and seed sets the scale: the smallest dishonour outweighs the largest standing. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both read kundri anaiya as 'even a kunrimani's weight'. Pope keeps the botanical sense: 'If meanness, slight as abrus grain, by men be wrought.' Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
புகழ்இன்றால் புத்தேள்நாட்டு உய்யாதால் என்மற்று
இகழ்வார்பின் சென்று நிலை.
transliteration:
Pugazhindraal puththelnaattu uyyaadhaal enmatru
Ikazhvaarpin sendru nilai.
current_meaning: Running after people who look down on you brings you no fame here and no place in heaven. So what good is it?
elementary: Some children follow around a bully who laughs at them, hoping to be liked. This kural asks: what do you get from that? Nobody admires it, and it does not make you a better person. Better to keep your self-respect.
university: The couplet is a rhetorical question built on the two goods of classical Tamil ethics: pugazh (புகழ், fame in this world) and puththel naadu (புத்தேள் நாடு, the land of the gods, i.e. heaven, reward in the next). Ikazhvaar pin sendru nilai (இகழ்வார்பின் சென்று நிலை), 'the state of going after those who scorn one', yields neither, hence en matru (என்மற்று), 'what else then?'. Solomon Pappaiah reads it as abandoning honour in order to live by following one's despisers. Kalaignar's gloss pointedly adds 'a heaven that does not exist', a modern rationalist reading; the older commentators take heaven at face value. Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
ஒட்டார்பின் சென்றொருவன் வாழ்தலின் அந்நிலையே
கெட்டான் எனப்படுதல் நன்று.
transliteration:
Ottaarpin sendroruvan vaazhdhalin annilaiye
Kettaan enappadudhal nandru.
current_meaning: It is better to be called a ruined person than to live by running after people who do not respect you.
elementary: Imagine choosing between staying poor but proud, or getting treats every day by doing whatever an unkind person tells you. This kural says it is better to lose the treats and keep your self-respect.
university: Ottaar (ஒட்டார்) are those who do not 'stick' to one: people who do not regard or accept one, or enemies. Living by following them (pin sendru vaazhdhal) is set against being called kettaan (கெட்டான், 'he is ruined', or 'he perished'). The phrase annilaiye (அந்நிலையே), 'in that very state', is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as remaining in one's own condition without stooping, while Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take kettaan more starkly as 'died'. Pope's English, quoted on ytamizh.com, follows the stronger reading: 'Better 'twere said, He's perished! than to gain / The means to live, following in foeman's train.' The couplet expresses a priority of honour over comfort, not an instruction to seek death. Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
மருந்தோமற்று ஊன்ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை பெருந்தகைமை
பீடழிய வந்த இடத்து.
transliteration:
Marundhomatru oonombum vaazhkkai perundhagaimai
Peedazhiya vandha idaththu.
current_meaning: When your honour and greatness are being destroyed, is just keeping your body alive some medicine that will save you from death forever?
elementary: Everyone grows old one day, no matter what. This kural asks: if you will not live forever anyway, why trade away your good name just to stay comfortable a little longer?
university: The rhetorical question marundho (மருந்தோ, 'is it a medicine?') implies a medicine against death (saavaamai, deathlessness), as Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both supply. Oon ombum vaazhkkai (ஊன் ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை) is a life that merely 'nourishes the flesh', set against perundhagaimai (பெருந்தகைமை, nobility) and peedu (பீடு, dignity, greatness), whose destruction is the occasion. The argument is that since death cannot be escaped, saving the body at the cost of honour gains nothing lasting. Kalaignar makes this explicit: there is no medicine for not dying, so do not lower your worth for a better life. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (some editions divide it மருந்தோமற் றூனோம்பும்).

tamil:
மயிர்நீப்பின் வாழாக் கவரிமா அன்னார்
உயிர்நீப்பர் மானம் வரின்.
transliteration:
Mayirneeppin vaazhaak kavarimaa annaar
Uyirneeppar maanam varin.
current_meaning: The yak is said to die if it loses its hair. Like that yak, people of honour would rather give up their life than live without honour.
elementary: An old story says the yak loves its long, beautiful hair so much it cannot live without it. This kural uses that story to say that some people treasure their good name the way the yak treasures its hair: nothing is worth losing it for.
university: The kavarimaa (கவரிமா) is the yak (Bos grunniens), whose tail-hair was prized for the chowrie or royal fly-whisk (chamara); popular Tamil usage later turned it into 'kavarimaan', a deer, though commentators identify it as the yak. The belief that it dies on losing its hair is poetic convention, not natural history; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as losing all its hair. Maanam varin (மானம் வரின்) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as 'if honour is about to be destroyed'. The Parimelazhagar tradition sees here the culmination of the chapter: honour valued above life. This is classical heroic ethics and should be read historically, as a statement of honour's supreme worth, not as a recommendation to end one's life; several traditions compared below explicitly reject taking one's own life. Text identical on both sources; Pope: 'Like the wild ox that, of its tuft bereft, will pine away.'

tamil:
இளிவரின் வாழாத மானம் உடையார்
ஒளிதொழுது ஏத்தும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Ilivarin vaazhaadha maanam udaiyaar
Olidhozhudhu eththum ulagu.
current_meaning: The world always bows to and praises the glory of honourable people who would rather die than live in shame.
elementary: People remember and admire heroes who never gave up doing what was right, even when it was very hard. This kural says the whole world keeps honouring such people long after they are gone.
university: Ilivu (இளிவு) is disgrace, humiliation; ilivarin vaazhaadha (இளிவரின் வாழாத) are those who 'do not live on when disgrace comes'. Oli (ஒளி), literally 'light', here means radiant fame, the glory that survives a person; Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss it as pugazh (புகழ்) or pugazh vadivu (the form of one's fame). Thozhudhu eththum (தொழுது ஏத்தும்) is the language of worship: folding hands and praising. The chapter closes where Tamil heroic ethics often closes, with lasting fame as the reward of honour. Read today, its lasting point is that the world reveres those who keep their integrity at great cost. Pope: 'Who, when dishonour comes, refuse to live, their honoured memory / Will live in worship and applause of all the world for aye!' Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
ஒளிஒருவற்கு உள்ள வெறுக்கை இளிஒருவற்கு
அஃதிறந்து வாழ்தும் எனல்.
transliteration:
Olioruvarku ulla verukkai ilioruvarku
ahdhirandhu vaazhdhum enal.
current_meaning: A person's true glory is a mind full of energy and drive. A person's shame is saying, 'I will get by without it.'
elementary: Some kids say, 'I will try the hard puzzle!' and their faces light up. Others say, 'I'll just skip it and sit.' Valluvar says the first kind of heart is what makes a person shine, and the lazy 'I'll just skip it' is what makes a person small.
university: The chapter opens by defining greatness as an inner quality rather than a rank: oli (ஒளி, 'light, lustre, renown') is ulla verukkai (உள்ள வெறுக்கை), literally 'the wealth/abundance of the mind', which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses as ஊக்கமிகுதி ('excess of zeal') and Puliyur Kesikan, following the older commentarial line descending from Parimelazhagar, as the resolve 'I will do what others find hard to do'. Its opposite, ili (இளி, 'disgrace'), is not failure but the attitude ahdhirandhu vaazhdhum enal (அஃதிறந்து வாழ்தும் எனல்), 'saying we shall live having let it go'. Pope's 'The light of life is mental energy' follows the majority reading; Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh reads verukkai as வெறுமை ('emptiness of mind'), a contemplative minority interpretation not shared by the classical glosses. Placed in the Kudiyiyal after Maanam (Honour, ch. 97), the chapter moves from guarding one's dignity to the active, self-effacing greatness of the noble. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பிறப்பொக்கும் எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் சிறப்பொவ்வா
செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமை யான்.
transliteration:
Pirappokkum ellaa uyirkkum sirappovvaa
seydhozhil vetrumai yaan.
current_meaning: All living beings are born the same way. They become different in worth only because of the different work they do.
elementary: Every baby is born the same way, crying and tiny, whether in a palace or a hut. What makes people different later is what they choose to do: who helps, who works hard, who is kind. That is where real specialness comes from.
university: The couplet sets piRappu (பிறப்பு, 'birth') against siRappu (சிறப்பு, 'distinction'): the first ஒக்கும் ('is equal') for all, the second ஒவ்வா ('is not equal') because of seydhozhil vetrumai (செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமை, 'difference in the work done'). Commentators differ on the scope of uyir: Puliyur Kesikan restricts it to 'all human lives' (எல்லா மக்களுயிர்க்கும்), the older reading, while modern glosses keep 'all living beings'. They also differ on tozhil: Mu. Varadarasanar speaks of the high and low grades of occupations, whereas Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as one's deeds or skill and make the verse an explicit statement that all are equal by birth. This egalitarian reading has made the couplet one of the most frequently cited in modern Tamil debates on caste. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மேலிருந்தும் மேலல்லார் மேலல்லர் கீழிருந்தும்
கீழல்லார் கீழல் லவர்.
transliteration:
Melirundhum melallaar melallar keezhirundhum
keezhallaar keezhal lavar.
current_meaning: Low people are not great even when they sit in high places. Good people are not low even when they are in low places.
elementary: Imagine a bully sitting on the tallest chair in class, and a kind child sitting on the floor. The tall chair does not make the bully great, and the floor does not make the kind child small. Who you are matters more than where you sit.
university: The verse is a chiasmus built on mel (மேல், 'above, superior') and keezh (கீழ், 'below, base'), each used both for physical or social position and for moral quality: melirundhum melallaar melallar, 'though they be above, those not superior are not superior'. Puliyur Kesikan makes the image literal, 'though they sit on high seats' (உயர்ந்த ஆசனங்களிலே), and ties superiority to having done 'deeds hard to do', linking back to Kural 971; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar render mel as high office or position. Pope's 'men of lofty line' reads it as birth, which carries the theme on from Kural 972. The repeated negatives (அல்லார், அல்லர், அல்லவர்) give the couplet its characteristic Valluvan density. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஒருமை மகளிரே போலப் பெருமையும்
தன்னைத்தான் கொண்டொழுகின் உண்டு.
transliteration:
Orumai magalire polap perumaiyum
thannaiththaan kondozhugin undu.
current_meaning: A faithful wife stays true by guarding herself. In the same way, greatness lasts only for a person who guards and controls themselves.
elementary: A promise only stays a promise if you keep it, even when nobody is watching. Valluvar says greatness is the same: it is not a prize someone hands you, it stays with you only while you keep guarding your own good behaviour.
university: The simile turns on orumai magalir (ஒருமை மகளிர், 'women of oneness'), which the commentators uniformly read as women of undivided chastity (கற்பு, karpu): Mu. Varadarasanar says ஒரு தன்மையான கற்புடைய மகளிர், and Puliyur Kesikan describes women whose minds do not waver and who guard themselves without lapsing. The point of comparison is thannaiththaan kondozhugin (தன்னைத்தான் கொண்டொழுகின், 'if one conducts oneself holding oneself'), that is, self-guarding: greatness, like chastity, cannot be imposed from outside and is lost by a single lapse. The gendered simile reflects the period; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it more inwardly as being true to oneself. Pope's 'Like single-hearted women, greatness too, / Exists while to itself is true' keeps the ambiguity. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பெருமை யுடையவர் ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றின்
அருமை உடைய செயல்.
transliteration:
Perumai yudaiyavar aatruvaar aatrin
arumai udaiya seyal.
current_meaning: People who have greatness will do, in the right way, things that are very hard for others to do.
elementary: Some jobs are so hard that most people give up, like building a tall tower of blocks without it falling. A great person keeps going and does it carefully, the right way, until it stands.
university: The verse plays on aatru (ஆற்று), used twice: aatruvaar ('they will accomplish') and aatrin, which commentators take either as 'by the (proper) way' (ஆறு, 'path, method') or as 'if they set about it'. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the first: 'in the way proper to it' (உரிய நெறியில்). Puliyur Kesikan adds 'even when they have fallen into poverty' (வறுமையான போதும்), the traditional gloss also reflected in Pope's explanation '(Though reduced) the great will be able to perform…', which holds that greatness shows itself in rare deeds even without resources. The couplet makes concrete the 'deeds hard for others' that Kural 971 called the light of a person. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
சிறியார் உணர்ச்சியுள் இல்லை பெரியாரைப்
பேணிக்கொள் வேமென்னும் நோக்கு.
transliteration:
Siriyaar unarchchiyul illai periyaaraip
penikkol vemennum nokku.
current_meaning: Small-minded people never have the thought, 'Let us respect great people and follow their ways.'
elementary: When a great teacher comes to school, some children run to listen and learn, hoping to become like her. Others just shrug and keep playing. Valluvar says wanting to learn from great people is itself a sign of a big heart.
university: Siriyaar (சிறியார், 'the small') is the counter-term to periyaar (பெரியார், 'the great') throughout this chapter and the next. The key phrase is peNikkoLvem (பேணிக்கொள்வேம், 'we will cherish and take to ourselves'): Puliyur Kesikan reads it as 'we will serve the great and attain their nature ourselves' (அவரியல்பை நாமும் அடைவோம்), Solomon Pappaiah as following them and preserving their tradition, and Mu. Varadarasanar as honouring them, which the small cannot do because they do not perceive the greatness at all. Nokku (நோக்கு, 'aim, outlook') and unarchchi (உணர்ச்சி, 'feeling, awareness') make the point psychological: the lack is in perception, not merely in will. Pope renders 'As votaries of the truly great we will ourselves enroll'. The text matches on both sites, with ytamizh omitting the final full stop.

tamil:
இறப்பே புரிந்த தொழிற்றாம் சிறப்புந்தான்
சீரல் லவர்கண் படின்.
transliteration:
Irappe purindha thozhitraam sirappundhaan
seeral lavarkan padin.
current_meaning: Even honour and high position, when they come to unworthy people, only make them act in ways that cross every limit.
elementary: Give a bossy child the job of class leader and he might start ordering everyone around and showing off. The badge was meant for helping, but in the wrong hands it turns into bullying.
university: Sirappu (சிறப்பு, 'eminence, distinction') here covers whatever raises a person; Solomon Pappaiah lists money, learning and office, and Pope's explanation 'nobility of birth, wealth and learning' reflects the traditional commentarial list. When it reaches seeral lavar (சீரல்லவர், 'those without worth'), it becomes irappe purindha thozhitru (இறப்பே புரிந்த தொழிற்று), 'of the nature of acting only in excess': irappu (இறப்பு) is taken by Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar as 'overstepping the bounds' (வரம்பு மீறிய செயல்) and by Kesikan as being driven into arrogance. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads irappu as 'destruction', a minority gloss. The couplet is the negative counterpart to Kural 975: the same eminence that lets the great do rare deeds makes the small insolent. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை சிறுமை
அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து.
transliteration:
Paniyumaam endrum perumai sirumai
aniyumaam thannai viyandhu.
current_meaning: Greatness always bows and stays modest. Smallness dresses itself up and admires itself.
elementary: A tree heavy with fruit bends its branches low, while an empty stalk sticks straight up. Valluvar says truly great people are like the fruit tree: they stay humble, while small people keep showing off.
university: The couplet sets two verbs in parallel, paniyum (பணியும், 'bends, submits') and aniyum (அணியும், 'adorns'), with the expletive -aam (ஆம்) giving the tone of a settled maxim and endrum (என்றும், 'always') applying to both. Thannai viyandhu (தன்னை வியந்து, 'admiring itself') explains the adorning: littleness dresses itself up in its own praise. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'greatness walks in humility at all times, littleness praises itself', and Kalaignar adds that the small lie puffed up (இறுமாந்து). Pope's 'Greatness humbly bends, but littleness always / Spreads out its plumes' turns aniyum into a peacock image not in the Tamil. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பெருமை பெருமிதம் இன்மை சிறுமை
பெருமிதம் ஊர்ந்து விடல்.
transliteration:
Perumai perumidham inmai sirumai
perumidham oorndhu vidal.
current_meaning: Greatness means not being full of pride. Smallness means riding high on pride and showing off.
elementary: A real champion says, 'Thanks, my team helped me.' Someone who isn't much of a champion struts around shouting, 'I'm the best!' Valluvar says being great means not puffing yourself up at all.
university: The couplet defines both terms through a single word, perumidham (பெருமிதம், 'swagger, pride'), which etymologically contains the same peru- ('great') as perumai: greatness is its absence (inmai, இன்மை), littleness is perumidham oorndhu vidal (பெருமிதம் ஊர்ந்து விடல்), 'mounting and riding on pride'. Mu. Varadarasanar reads oorndhu vidal as 'pride growing until it reaches its limit and stopping there', while Solomon Pappaiah sharpens the contrast: having cause for pride yet not being proud is greatness, being proud without cause is littleness. Pope's 'Riding on car of vanity supreme' keeps the image of mounting a vehicle. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அற்றம் மறைக்கும் பெருமை சிறுமைதான்
குற்றமே கூறி விடும்.
transliteration:
Atram maraikkum perumai sirumaidhaan
kutrame koori vidum.
current_meaning: Greatness hides other people's weak points. Smallness talks about nothing but their faults.
elementary: If a friend trips and falls in the playground, a kind person helps them up and doesn't laugh. A mean person runs around telling everyone, 'Did you see him fall?' Valluvar says greatness is the helping hand, and smallness is the tattletale.
university: Atram (அற்றம்) means a weak, exposed or shameful point, literally a gap or defenceless state; maraikkum (மறைக்கும்) is 'conceals'. Against this, sirumai kutrame kooRi vidum (குற்றமே கூறி விடும்): 'littleness will speak out only faults', the emphatic -e (ஏ) on kutram marking that it says nothing else. Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah expand the contrast: the great speak of others' merits and hide their failings, the small hide their merits and broadcast their failings. Pope's 'Greatness will hide a neighbour's shame; / Meanness his faults to all the world proclaim' follows this reading. The chapter thus ends on how the great treat others, after nine couplets on how they hold themselves. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கடன்என்ப நல்லவை எல்லாம் கடன்அறிந்து
சான்றாண்மை மேற்கொள் பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Kadanenpa nallavai ellaam kadanarindhu
saandraanmai merkol pavarkku.
current_meaning: For people who know their duty and choose to live with perfect character, all good things are said to be simply part of their duty.
elementary: Some children help clear the table only when someone asks and then want a sticker for it. Others just do it every day because that is who they are. Valluvar says truly good people are like the second kind: being kind and helpful is not an extra for them, it is just their everyday job.
university: The chapter title saandraanmai (சான்றாண்மை, from saandror, 'the full, the accomplished', and aanmai, 'mastery, the bearing of a quality') names the fullness of noble character; the related noun saalbu (சால்பு, 'abundance, completeness') recurs throughout the chapter. The opening couplet turns on kadan (கடன், 'debt, duty'): for one who knows his kadan and undertakes (merkol, மேற்கொள்) saandraanmai, all good things (nallavai ellaam) are themselves called duty. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses that for such a person all good things become 'natural duty' (இயல்பான கடமை), and Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan both render it as good qualities becoming one's very nature, the line of interpretation that follows the traditional commentary of Parimelazhagar, in which virtue is no longer a burden chosen case by case but an obligation already accepted. Pope's 'All goodly things are duties to the men, they say' keeps the reported-speech force of enpa (என்ப, 'they say'), marking this as received wisdom. Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh reverses the predicate ('the obligatory duty is the good things'), a minor variation in emphasis rather than in sense. The chapter follows Perumai (Greatness, ch. 98) in the Kudiyiyal and is followed by Panbudaimai (Courtesy, ch. 100). The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
குணநலம் சான்றோர் நலனே பிறநலம்
எந்நலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று.
transliteration:
Kunanalam saandror nalane piranalam
ennalaththu ulladhooum andru.
current_meaning: The true goodness of noble people is the goodness of their character. No other kind of goodness counts as real goodness at all.
elementary: A shiny new bike, a nice haircut or a fancy pair of shoes can look great. But Valluvar says the thing that really makes a person beautiful is a kind and honest heart. Everything else is just wrapping paper.
university: The couplet sets kunanalam (குணநலம், 'the goodness of qualities, beauty of character') against piranalam (பிறநலம், 'other goods'). The noble (saandror) have only one nalam (நலம், 'good, beauty, excellence') worth the name; the other kinds are not counted 'among any good' (ennalaththu ulladhooum andru, எந்நலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று), where ulladhooum shows the alapedai (vowel lengthening) that fills out the metre. Solomon Pappaiah and Mu. Karunanidhi read nalam as beauty (அழகு), contrasting inner beauty of character with outward beauty of form, while Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the more general 'good'; Pope's prose rendering, following the older commentarial tradition associated with Parimelazhagar, understands the other goods as sensual delights. Both readings make the same claim: for the perfected person only character counts. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அன்புநாண் ஒப்புரவு கண்ணோட்டம் வாய்மையொடு
ஐந்துசால் ஊன்றிய தூண்.
transliteration:
Anbunaan oppuravu kannottam vaaimaiyodu
aindhusaal oondriya thoon.
current_meaning: Love, shame at doing wrong, helping everyone, kindness toward others, and truthfulness: these five are the pillars that hold up perfect character.
elementary: Think of a tree house held up by five strong posts. If one post breaks, the house wobbles. Valluvar says a good person is held up by five posts too: loving others, feeling shy about doing wrong, sharing, being kind, and telling the truth.
university: This is the chapter's architectural image: saalbu (perfection) is a load resting on five pillars (aindhu ... oondriya thoon, ஐந்து ... ஊன்றிய தூண்). The five are anbu (அன்பு, 'affection'), naan (நாண், 'shame', specifically recoil from blameworthy deeds, as Pappaiah glosses பழி பாவங்களுக்கு நாணுதல்), oppuravu (ஒப்புரவு, 'benevolence to all, sharing what one has gathered', the subject of ch. 22), kannottam (கண்ணோட்டம், 'kindly regard', literally 'running of the eye', the subject of ch. 58) and vaaimai (வாய்மை, 'truthfulness', ch. 30). Commentators differ on how to parse saal: most take ஐந்து சால்பு ஊன்றிய தூண் as 'the five pillars that bear saalbu', while Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as pillars of the 'vessel' of perfection; Pope renders 'pillars five of perfect virtue's resting-place'. Karunanidhi glosses oppuravu as 'honouring the world's conduct' and kannottam as 'compassionate acts', showing how the virtues shade into each other. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கொல்லா நலத்தது நோன்மை பிறர்தீமை
சொல்லா நலத்தது சால்பு.
transliteration:
Kollaa nalaththadhu nonmai pirardheemai
sollaa nalaththadhu saalbu.
current_meaning: Self-discipline is built on the goodness of not killing. Perfect character is built on the goodness of not talking about other people's wrongs.
elementary: A good person does not hurt any living creature, not even a bug. And a really good person also does not go around telling everyone the bad things someone else did. Valluvar says the first is the heart of being holy, and the second is the heart of being truly good.
university: A balanced couplet built on two parallel phrases: kollaa nalam (கொல்லா நலம், 'the goodness of not killing') grounds nonmai (நோன்மை, 'austerity, penance', glossed as தவம் by Varadarasanar and Kesikan), while sollaa nalam (சொல்லா நலம், 'the goodness of not telling') grounds saalbu. Pirar theemai (பிறர்தீமை) may mean either others' faults or the wrongs others have done; Karunanidhi takes the second ('not pointing out the harm others do'), the majority the first. The pairing ties this chapter to Kollaamai (ch. 33) and Purangooraamai (Not Backbiting, ch. 19), and suggests that just as non-killing is the essence of the ascetic, refusal to broadcast faults is the essence of the noble householder. Pope's 'penitence' for nonmai is archaic; 'austerity' is closer. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads nonmai more broadly as 'sustaining life without destroying'. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பணிதல் அதுசான்றோர்
மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை.
transliteration:
Aatruvaar aatral panidhal adhusaandror
maatraarai maatrum padai.
current_meaning: The strength of capable people is their modesty. It is the weapon good people use to turn their enemies into friends.
elementary: When someone is cross with you, shouting back usually makes it worse. But if you speak gently and say sorry, the angry person often calms down and even becomes your friend. Valluvar says being humble is the strongest tool a good person has.
university: The couplet plays on the root aatru (ஆற்று, 'to accomplish, to be able'): aatruvaar aatral (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல்), 'the power of those who can achieve', is panidhal (பணிதல், 'bending, humility'). In the second line maatraar (மாற்றார், 'adversaries') are 'changed' (maatrum, மாற்றும்) by this padai (படை, 'weapon, army'), a deliberate pun. Most modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Karunanidhi) read the second line as humility turning enemies away from enmity; Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan, nearer the older commentarial line of Parimelazhagar, read the first line more concretely as the achiever's skill in winning over helpers by bowing to them. Pope's 'Submission is the might of men of mighty acts; the sage / With that same weapon stills his foeman's rage' captures both senses. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
சால்பிற்குக் கட்டளை யாதெனின் தோல்வி
துலையல்லார் கண்ணும் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Saalbirkuk kattalai yaadhenin tholvi
thulaiyallaar kannum kolal.
current_meaning: If you ask what the test of perfect character is, it is being willing to accept defeat even from people who are not your equals.
elementary: It is easy to say 'You win' to a big champion. It is much harder to say it to a younger child who beat you at a game. Valluvar says being able to lose gracefully, even to someone smaller, is the real test of a good person.
university: Kattalai (கட்டளை) here is the touchstone (உரைகல்) used to test gold, as Varadarasanar and Pappaiah gloss it: saalbu is gold, and its test is tholvi ... kolal (தோல்வி ... கொளல், 'accepting defeat'). Thulai allaar (துலையல்லார்), literally 'those not of the same balance (thulai, துலை)', are one's inferiors; the particle -um in kannum (கண்ணும், 'even with') makes the point that yielding to a superior is no test at all. Kesikan spells out the contrast: the defeat one would accept from one's betters must be accepted even from lesser people. Pope's verse ('What is perfection's test? The equal mind. / To bear repulse from even meaner men resigned') introduces 'equal mind' as a gloss rather than a translation. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads thulaiyallaar as those 'unfit to accept defeat', a less common construal. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இன்னாசெய் தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்
என்ன பயத்ததோ சால்பு.
transliteration:
Innaasey thaarkkum iniyave seyyaakkaal
enna payaththadho saalbu.
current_meaning: What use is perfect character if it does not do kind things even to people who have hurt you?
elementary: Being nice to people who are nice to you is easy. Valluvar asks a harder question: what if someone was mean to you? He says that being kind back to them is what really shows you are a good person.
university: The couplet is a rhetorical question: if one does not do iniyavai (இனியவை, 'pleasant, kind things') even to those who did innaa (இன்னா, 'painful, harmful things'), of what use (enna payaththadho, என்ன பயத்ததோ) is saalbu? The -um of thaarkkum (தார்க்கும், 'even to those who did') carries the force. It restates for the noble householder the teaching of Innaa Seyyaamai (ch. 32), especially Kural 314 (inna seydhaarai oruththal avar naana nannayam seydhu vidal), and all modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Karunanidhi, Kesikan) agree on the plain sense. Note that the English section for this couplet on ytamizh.com is misaligned: its 'Couplet Explanation' belongs to Kural 946 on overeating and the line printed as the couplet is Pope's prose explanation, so it should not be relied on here. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று சால்பென்னும்
திண்மைஉண் டாகப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Inmai oruvarku ilivandru saalbennum
thinmaiun daakap perin.
current_meaning: Being poor is no shame for a person who has the inner strength called perfect character.
elementary: Some people have lots of toys and money, and some have very little. Valluvar says having little is nothing to be ashamed of, as long as you are honest, kind and strong inside. That inner strength is worth more than any treasure.
university: Inmai (இன்மை, 'having nothing, poverty') is not ilivu (இளிவு, 'disgrace') for one who has gained the thinmai (திண்மை, 'firmness, solidity') called saalbu. The image of perfection as a kind of solidity anticipates the stability of Kural 989. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Karunanidhi all read inmai as material poverty, and Karunanidhi adds that such a person treats saalbu itself as wealth; Sivayogi Sivakumar widens inmai to 'hardships'. Textual note: ytamizh.com reads இளிவன்று (ilivandru, 'is not disgrace'), the standard reading supported by the commentaries' gloss இழிவு; thirukkural.net's main text prints இனிவன்று, which appears to be a typographical error (ன for ள), since its own commentaries gloss the word as இழிவு. This edition follows இளிவன்று. Placed just before the chapters on Nalkuravu (Poverty, ch. 105) and Iravu (Begging, ch. 106), the couplet establishes that character, not wealth, sets the limits of dignity.

tamil:
ஊழி பெயரினும் தாம்பெயரார் சான்றாண்மைக்கு
ஆழி எனப்படு வார்.
transliteration:
Oozhi peyarinum thaampeyaraar saandraanmaikku
aazhi enappadu vaar.
current_meaning: People who are called the ocean of perfect character will not change, even if the great ages of the world come to an end and change.
elementary: A big rock on the beach stays in the same place year after year while the waves, the weather and the people all change around it. Valluvar says truly good people are like that: whatever happens around them, they stay good.
university: Oozhi (ஊழி) is the cosmic age or aeon, and its 'shifting' (peyarinum, பெயரினும், 'even if it moves') evokes the dissolution at the end of an age, when, in Indian cosmology, the seas break their bounds. Against this, those called aazhi (ஆழி) of saandraanmai do not shift (thaam peyaraar, தாம்பெயரார்). Aazhi can mean either 'ocean' or 'shore, boundary', and the commentators divide: Varadarasanar and Karunanidhi take it as ocean ('the ocean of perfection'), while Pappaiah and Kesikan, with Pope ('of perfect virtue's sea the shore'), read it as the shore that holds the sea in, an image which sharpens the contrast, since the shore holds even when the seas of the age-end overflow. Pope's line 'Who, though the fates should fail' renders oozhi loosely as fate. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads oozhi as ordinary change over time. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
சான்றவர் சான்றாண்மை குன்றின் இருநிலந்தான்
தாங்காது மன்னோ பொறை.
transliteration:
Saandravar saandraanmai kundrin irunilandhaan
thaangaadhu manno porai.
current_meaning: If good people ever lost their goodness, even this great earth could not carry its own weight.
elementary: Imagine a big table held up by a few strong legs. If those legs get weak, everything on the table comes crashing down. Valluvar says good people are like those legs for the whole world: if they stop being good, the world cannot hold itself up.
university: The closing couplet extends saandraanmai from personal virtue to cosmic support. If the saandravar (சான்றவர், 'the perfected') should decline (kundrin, குன்றின்) in their saandraanmai, the 'great earth' (irunilam, இருநிலம்) itself could not bear (thaangaadhu, தாங்காது) its porai (பொறை, 'burden'); manno (மன்னோ) is an emphatic particle. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kesikan read porai as the earth's burden, so that the noble become, with the five pillars of Kural 983, the hidden supports of the world; Karunanidhi instead takes porai as 'patience', reading that the world would not patiently tolerate such a decline. Sivayogi Sivakumar's reading of irunilam as the 'two states' of inner and outer life is idiosyncratic. Pope: 'The mighty earth its burthen to sustain must cease, / If perfect virtue of the perfect men decrease.' The idea that the righteous sustain the world appears in many traditions, and here completes the chapter's arc from personal duty (981) to the stability of the world. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
எண்பதத்தால் எய்தல் எளிதென்ப யார்மாட்டும்
பண்புடைமை என்னும் வழக்கு.
transliteration:
Enpadhaththaal eydhal elidhenpa yaarmaattum
panputaimai ennum vazhakku.
current_meaning: People say that being easy for anyone to approach makes it easy to gain the good way called courtesy (being polite and kind to all).
elementary: Imagine a class helper whose door is always open, who smiles at every kid, big or small, and listens. Being kind and polite is easy for that helper because they already let everyone come close. Valluvar says good manners grow out of being easy to reach.
