university: The chapter on panbudaimai (பண்புடைமை, 'possession of refined character, courtesy') opens with a practical claim: the path is easy for the one who has en-padham (எண்பதம்), 'easy access', the quality of being approachable (எளிய செவ்வி) to everyone, yaar-maattum (யார்மாட்டும், 'towards whomsoever'). Puliyur Kesikan on thirukkural.net and Mu. Varadarasanar on ytamizh both gloss en-padham as எளிய செவ்வி, availability to all comers, and vazhakku (வழக்கு) as the established good path or usage; Solomon Pappaiah adds that the claim is reported, 'say the learned' (நூலோர் கூறுவர்), reflecting the verb enpa (என்ப, 'they say'). Sivayogi Sivakumar's reading of en as 'numbers' (speaking in words as plain as numerals) is an idiosyncratic minority interpretation not shared by the classical glosses. Pope renders the couplet 'Who easy access give to every man, they say, / Of kindly courtesy will learn with ease the way', and the same accessibility motif appears in the earlier kural 386 on the king who is kaatchikku eliyan (easy of audience). Placed in the Kudiyiyal after Saanraanmai (ch. 99), the chapter turns from the inner perfection of the noble to its outward social face. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல் இவ்விரண்டும்
பண்புடைமை என்னும் வழக்கு.
transliteration:
Anputaimai aandra kutippiraththal ivvirantum
panputaimai ennum vazhakku.
current_meaning: Love for others and being born into a good family: these two together make up the way called courtesy.
elementary: Think of a kind heart as the seed and a good home as the garden it grows in. When a child has both a loving heart and a family that teaches good ways, gentle manners bloom. Valluvar says courtesy needs both.
university: The second couplet names the two roots of panbudaimai: anbudaimai (அன்புடைமை, 'possession of love', the title of chapter 8) and aandra kudip-piraththal (ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல், 'being born in an eminent, accomplished family'). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take aandra kudi as a high or noble family, while Solomon Pappaiah reinterprets it as a family that 'lives in harmony with the world' (உலகத்தோடு ஒத்து வாழும் குடும்பம்), softening the hereditary emphasis; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as living a birth worth reflecting on. Pope's 'Benevolence and high born dignity, / These two are beaten paths of courtesy' preserves vazhakku (வழக்கு) as a 'beaten path' or established usage. The kural links this chapter back to Kudimai (ch. 96, 'Nobility of family'), which places good family upbringing at the base of character; modern readers often stress that the second element is about formation and tradition rather than caste rank. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உறுப்பொத்தல் மக்களொப்பு அன்றால் வெறுத்தக்க
பண்பொத்தல் ஒப்பதாம் ஒப்பு.
transliteration:
Uruppoththal makkaloppu andraal veruththakka
panpoththal oppadhaam oppu.
current_meaning: Having the same body parts does not make people truly alike. Being alike in good, pleasing character is the real likeness.
elementary: Two dolls can look exactly the same on the outside, but one might be stuffed with cotton and the other with sharp pins. People are like that too: having two eyes and two hands like someone does not make you like them. Being kind like them does.
university: Uruppu-oththal (உறுப்பொத்தல், 'sameness of limbs') is denied the status of makkal-oppu (மக்களொப்பு, 'likeness among humans'); true oppu is panb-oththal (பண்பொத்தல்), likeness in qualities. The crux is veruththakka (வெறுத்தக்க): Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as 'fit to be joined' (பொருந்தத்தக்க), Solomon Pappaiah as qualities that unite heart with heart, and Pope as 'kindred quality' ('Similitude of kindred quality makes likeness true'), reflecting the older commentarial reading of வெறு as 'to be close, to cohere'. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads it in the modern sense 'hateful', yielding 'likeness in shunning what deserves shunning', a minority interpretation. Kalaignar draws the strong conclusion that only those alike in good qualities deserve to be counted as human at all, which anticipates kural 997. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நயனொடு நன்றி புரிந்த பயனுடையார்
பண்புபா ராட்டும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Nayanotu nandri purindha payanutaiyaar
panpupaa raattum ulaku.
current_meaning: The world praises the character of people who are useful to others because they are fair and do good.
elementary: When a kid is fair in games and also helps others when they fall, everyone on the playground says, 'She's so nice!' Valluvar says people love and praise those who are both fair and helpful.
university: The couplet pairs nayan (நயன், 'justice, equity, fairness') with nanri (நன்றி, 'beneficence, doing good'), and calls those who 'cherish' (purindha, புரிந்த) both payan-udaiyaar (பயனுடையார்), people who are of real use to others. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the pair as நீதியும் நன்மையும், Pappaiah as நீதியும் அறமும், and Pope's prose 'equity and charity' follows the same traditional line. The result is that ulagu (உலகு, 'the world', i.e. the discerning public) 'praises' (paaraattum, பாராட்டும்) their panbu. Sivayogi Sivakumar takes nayan as conduct that gives delight, a looser reading. The kural shows that courtesy in Valluvar is not mere politeness of speech but includes just and beneficial action. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நகையுள்ளும் இன்னா திகழ்ச்சி பகையுள்ளும்
பண்புள பாடறிவார் மாட்டு.
transliteration:
Nakaiyullum innaa thikazhchchi pakaiyullum
panpula paadarivaar maattu.
current_meaning: Making fun of someone hurts, even as a joke. So people who understand others stay polite even toward their enemies.
elementary: Calling someone a silly name 'just for fun' can still make them cry inside. Kids who really understand feelings don't do it, not even to a kid they're cross with. Valluvar says being polite even to someone you don't like is a sign of real wisdom.
university: The first line states a psychological fact: igazhchi (இகழ்ச்சி, 'contempt, ridicule') is innaa (இன்னா, 'painful') even within nagai (நகை, 'laughter, jest'). The second draws the ethical conclusion: among paadarivaar (பாடறிவார், 'those who know the nature or proper manner', from பாடு, 'way, condition'), panbu remains even within pagai (பகை, 'enmity'). Mu. Varadarasanar reads the paadarivaar as those who act knowing others' nature; Pappaiah expands that such people do not ridicule even foes; Pope renders 'Contempt is evil though in sport. They who man's nature know, / E'en in their wrath, a courteous mind will show.' The jingle nagaiyullum ... pagaiyullum binds jest and enmity as the two tests of courtesy. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டுண்டு உலகம் அதுஇன்றேல்
மண்புக்கு மாய்வது மன்.
transliteration:
Panputaiyaarp pattuntu ulakam adhuindrel
manpukku maaivadhu man.
current_meaning: The world keeps going because good-mannered people live in it. Without them, it would sink into the earth and die away.
elementary: A tent stands up because of its poles. Take the poles away and the whole tent falls flat on the ground. Valluvar says kind, well-mannered people are the poles that hold up the whole world.
university: Ulagam (உலகம்) here means the ongoing life of human society; it 'exists' (undu, உண்டு) because it is pattu (பட்டு, 'resting upon, attached to') the panbudaiyaar (பண்புடையார், 'people of character'). Without that support it would man-pukku maaivadhu (மண்புக்கு மாய்வது), 'enter the earth and perish', the final man (மன்) being an emphatic particle. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses pattu as 'by being joined to' the courteous; Kalaignar reads ulagam as 'the conduct of the world'; Pope's prose 'The (way of the) world subsists by contact with the good' follows the traditional line. Sivayogi Sivakumar takes the second line very differently, as 'even supplication would be meaningless', which departs from the classical gloss of man-pukku as 'entering the soil'. The kural echoes kural 571 on kannottam, where the world exists through the gracious. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அரம்போலும் கூர்மைய ரேனும் மரம்போல்வர்
மக்கட்பண்பு இல்லா தவர்.
transliteration:
Arampolum koormaiya renum marampolvar
makkatpanpu illaa thavar.
current_meaning: People without good human qualities are no better than trees, even if their minds are as sharp as a file (a metal tool for sharpening).
elementary: A pencil sharpener is very sharp, but it can't give you a hug or say sorry. Valluvar says a person can be super clever, but if they aren't kind they are like a tree trunk: standing there, but not really acting like a person.
university: The couplet plays on the rhyme aram (அரம், 'file, rasp') and maram (மரம், 'tree'): those who lack makkat-panbu (மக்கட்பண்பு, 'the quality proper to human beings') are 'like trees' even if they have a file's koormai (கூர்மை, 'sharpness'). Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah both gloss maram as ஓரறிவுயிர், 'a one-sensed being', invoking the classical Tamil (and Jain) grading of living beings by the number of their senses, so the insult is precise: an intellect without humanity sinks to the lowest rung of life. Pope renders 'Though sharp their wit as file, as blocks they must remain, / Whose souls are void of courtesy humane'. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads aram as a sharp cutting tool and makkat-panbu as 'humanitarianism'. The kural extends the argument of 993 from likeness to humanity itself. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நண்பாற்றார் ஆகி நயமில செய்வார்க்கும்
பண்பாற்றார் ஆதல் கடை.
transliteration:
Nanpaatraar aaki nayamila seyvaarkkum
panpaatraar aadhal katai.
current_meaning: Even toward people who are unfriendly and do us wrong, failing to be polite is the lowest thing a person can do.
elementary: If a classmate keeps being mean to you, it is tempting to be mean back. But Valluvar says the really strong thing is to stay polite anyway. Being rude back would make you lose something precious of your own.
university: The couplet carries the chapter's ethic to its hardest case. Nanb-aatraar (நண்பாற்றார்) are those who 'do not practise friendship', and nayam-ila seyvaar (நயமில செய்வார்) those who 'do unpleasant, unjust things'; even toward them, to be panb-aatraar (பண்பாற்றார், 'not practising courtesy') is kadai (கடை), 'the lowest, the worst'. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it as a disgrace (இழிவு) to abandon courtesy in the face of hostility; Kalaignar adds patience (பொறுமை) as the means. Pope's 'Though men with all unfriendly acts and wrongs assail, / 'Tis uttermost disgrace in courtesy to fail' captures the parallel of nanbaatraar ... panbaatraar. The kural echoes kural 314 on 'shaming' wrongdoers by doing them good. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நகல்வல்லர் அல்லார்க்கு மாயிரு ஞாலம்
பகலும்பாற் பட்டன்று இருள்.
transliteration:
Nakalvallar allaarkku maayiru gnaalam
pakalumpaar pattandru irul.
current_meaning: For people who cannot enjoy friendly, cheerful company, this huge wide world is dark even in the middle of the day.
elementary: Imagine a sunny day at the park, but you won't play, laugh, or talk with anyone. Even with the sun shining, it would feel gloomy. Valluvar says a heart that can't smile and join in makes the whole world feel dark.
university: Nagal vallar allaar (நகல்வல்லர் அல்லார்) are 'those not able to laugh', that is, unable to mix with others and share friendly cheer; for them maa-iru gnaalam (மாயிரு ஞாலம், 'the great, vast earth') is, even by day (pagalum), fallen into darkness (paal patta-andru irul, பாற்பட்டன்று இருள்). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses nagal as 'mingling with others and rejoicing' (பிறரோடு கலந்து பழகி மகிழ), Pappaiah ties it explicitly to lack of good character, and Kalaignar to inability to enjoy friends; Pope's prose 'To those who cannot rejoice, the wide world is buried darkness even in (broad) day light' follows this line. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads nagal as 'harmonizing with others' and iru as 'two-fold', an idiosyncratic segmentation. The transliteration of gnaalam varies across sites (Gnaalam on ytamizh, ñālam on thirukkural.net). The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பண்பிலான் பெற்ற பெருஞ்செல்வம் நன்பால்
கலந்தீமை யால்திரிந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Panpilaan petra perunjelvam nanpaal
kalandheemai yaaldhirin thatru.
current_meaning: Great riches that come to a person without good manners are like good milk spoiled by a dirty pot.
elementary: Pour fresh milk into a dirty cup and it turns sour and yucky. Valluvar says money is like that milk: if it goes to a rude, unkind person, it turns sour and does nobody any good.
university: The chapter closes with a domestic simile: the perum-selvam (பெருஞ்செல்வம், 'great wealth') of the panbilaan (பண்பிலான், 'man without courtesy') is like nan-paal (நன்பால், 'good milk') that has 'turned' (thirindhu, திரிந்து) through kalam-theemai (கலந்தீமை, 'defect of the vessel'). Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read kalan as the container (கலம், பாத்திரம்), Kalaignar specifying a vessel coated with verdigris (களிம்பு); Pope's verse 'Like sweet milk soured because in filthy vessel poured' agrees, while his prose 'will perish like pure milk spoilt by the impurity of the vessel' stresses waste. The segmentation kalan + theemai, rather than kalandhu + theemai ('mixed with evil'), is the standard one; Sivayogi Sivakumar's 'by the evil mixed with it' reflects the alternative split. The kural also bridges to the next chapter, Nanriyil Selvam (ch. 101, 'Useless wealth'). Transliterations differ slightly (yaaldhirinh thatru on ytamizh; yaaldhirin thatru on thirukkural.net), but the Tamil text is identical on both sites.

tamil:
வைத்தான்வாய் சான்ற பெரும்பொருள் அஃதுண்ணான்
செத்தான் செயக்கிடந்தது இல்.
transliteration:
Vaiththaanvaai Saandra Perumporul Aqdhunnaan
Seththaan Seyakkitandhadhu Il
current_meaning: A person who fills their house with huge riches but never uses them is as good as dead, because those riches do nothing at all.
elementary: Imagine a boy who fills his whole room with sweets but never eats one and never shares one. The sweets just sit there until they go stale. Valluvar says a person who piles up money like that and never uses it might as well not be there at all.
university: The chapter title நன்றியில் செல்வம் uses நன்றி in its older sense of 'benefit, good' rather than 'gratitude': this is wealth that does no good to anyone. In vaittaan-vaay (வைத்தான்வாய்) வாய் means 'place', so the wealth 'fills the place where he stored it'; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses இடமெல்லாம் நிறைந்த, and Puliyur Kesikan (thirukkural.net) adds that the man does not eat it 'through avarice' (உலோபத்தால்). The second line is elliptical: seththaan (செத்தான்) can be read either as 'he is (equivalent to) a dead man', as Solomon Pappaiah and Pope take it ('Is dead'), or as 'when he dies, there is nothing left done (by the wealth)', as Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar render it; both readings yield the same verdict that unused wealth achieves nothing. The chapter stands in the Kudiyiyal after Panbudaimai (ch. 100), turning from courtesy to the social uselessness of hoarded riches, and complements the earlier chapters on Ithal (ch. 23) and Oppuravu (ch. 22). The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பொருளானாம் எல்லாமென்று ஈயாது இவறும்
மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Porulaanaam Ellaamendru Eeyaadhu Ivarum
Marulaanaam Maanaap Pirappu
current_meaning: Thinking money can do everything, a person holds it tight and gives nothing away. That foolish mistake leads to a low, worthless birth.
elementary: Some people think, 'If I just have enough money, I'll have everything!' So they grip their money tight and never share. Valluvar says this is a big mistake, like a confused traveller holding the wrong map, and it leads them to a very sad place.
university: The first line reports the miser's creed, poruLaal aam ellaam ('by wealth everything is achieved'), and his conduct, eeyaadhu ivaRum ('not giving, he clings'); ivaRu- denotes tight-fisted holding, the same root as இவறல் (miserliness) condemned among royal faults in Kural 432. The second line names the result: maruL (மருள், 'delusion, bewilderment') produces maaNaap piRappu, 'an un-excellent birth'. Mu. Varadarasanar keeps this general ('a birth without distinction'), Kalaignar reads it this-worldly ('a base creature'), while Solomon Pappaiah and Pope's explanation ('will be born a demon') follow the classical line that specifies a ghost or demon birth (பேய்ப் பிறப்பு); Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as an endless, graceless cycle of births. The phrase மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு also closes Kural 351, where delusion about what is real is said to cause such a birth, so Valluvar here treats the miser's faith in money as a species of metaphysical error. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஈட்டம் இவறி இசைவேண்டா ஆடவர்
தோற்றம் நிலக்குப் பொறை.
transliteration:
Eettam Ivari Isaiventaa Aatavar
Thotram Nilakkup Porai
current_meaning: People who only want to pile up money and do not care about a good name are just a weight on the earth.
elementary: Think of a squirrel that hides a thousand nuts and never lets another animal have one, and no one in the forest has a kind word for it. Valluvar says people who only collect and collect, and never do anything good that others would remember, are just heavy weight on the ground.
university: The couplet sets two objects of desire against each other: eettam (ஈட்டம், 'accumulation', from ஈட்டு- 'to earn, amass') and isai (இசை, 'fame, renown'), which in the Kural is earned chiefly by giving (compare Pugazh, ch. 24, beginning 'ஈதல் இசைபட வாழ்தல்'). Those who 'cling to accumulation and do not want renown' have a thoatram (தோற்றம், 'appearance, birth, existence') that is poRai (பொறை, 'burden, weight') to the earth; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read தோற்றம் as 'being born and living', Pope as appearing 'on the stage of being'. Solomon Pappaiah adds a competitive nuance: they want to amass more than others. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads இசை as 'interest/inclination' (இசைவு) beyond acquiring wealth, a minority interpretation. The 'burden of the earth' image echoes Kural 239, where the land bearing a body without fame loses its yield. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
எச்சமென்று என்எண்ணுங் கொல்லோ ஒருவரால்
நச்சப் படாஅ தவன்.
transliteration:
Echchamendru Enennung Kollo Oruvaraal
Nachchap Pataaa Thavan
current_meaning: What does a person whom no one loves think they will leave behind after they die?
elementary: When a kind teacher retires, the children remember her stories and her hugs for years. But if someone never helped anyone, what will people remember about him when he is gone? Valluvar asks: what is left of a person nobody loved?
university: The key word is echcham (எச்சம், 'remainder, what is left over'), which in the Kural can mean posterity or a lasting name; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss 'what remains after his death', Solomon Pappaiah 'what will stand to recall him after his time'. The man is described as oruvaraal nachchap padaaa-thavan, 'one not desired by even a single person'; nachchu (நச்சு, 'to desire, love') returns in Kural 1008, where the same unloved man's wealth is a poisonous tree, so the chapter plays on நச்சு 'love' and நச்சு 'poison'. Mu. Varadarasanar supplies the reason for his unpopularity, that he helped no one. Pope's explanation narrows echcham to what the miser can count as his own 'in the world to come', a reading that follows the classical tendency to interpret legacy in terms of merit for the next life. The rhetorical question (என் எண்ணும் கொல்லோ, 'what, pray, does he think?') turns the couplet into a mock of the miser's planning. The text is identical on both sources (ytamizh prints எண்ணுங் with the same ங்).

tamil:
கொடுப்பதூஉம் துய்ப்பதூஉம் இல்லார்க்கு அடுக்கிய
கோடியுண் டாயினும் இல்.
transliteration:
Kotuppadhooum Thuyppadhooum Illaarkku Atukkiya
Kotiyun Taayinum Il
current_meaning: For people who neither give their money away nor enjoy it themselves, even crores upon crores (huge piles of money) are as good as nothing.
elementary: If you have a big box of crayons but never draw with them and never lend them to a friend, it is just like having no crayons at all. Valluvar says money works the same way: if you never use it and never share it, you are really poor.
university: The couplet names the two proper uses of wealth, koduppadhu (கொடுப்பது, 'giving') and thuyppadhu (துய்ப்பது, 'enjoying, consuming'), with the emphatic lengthening -ūum (கொடுப்பதூஉம், துய்ப்பதூஉம்) marking each as indispensable. Adukkiya kodi (அடுக்கிய கோடி) means 'crores stacked one upon another'; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'many crores ever increasing'. The verdict il (இல், 'there is not') says such people are effectively without wealth; Pope renders the sense as 'they are poor'. Solomon Pappaiah adds the qualifier that giving should be to those in need and enjoying should be as need requires, guarding against reading the couplet as licence for extravagance. The two-fold scheme parallels the Sanskrit gnomic triad of dāna, bhoga and nāśa (giving, enjoyment, destruction) found in Bhartrihari. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஏதம் பெருஞ்செல்வம் தான்துவ்வான் தக்கார்க்கொன்று
ஈதல் இயல்பிலா தான்.
transliteration:
Edham Perunjelvam Thaandhuvvaan Thakkaarkkondru
Eedhal Iyalpilaa Thaan
current_meaning: A person who does not enjoy their great riches, and does not have it in their nature to give some to people who deserve it, is like a sickness to those riches.
elementary: Imagine a lovely garden where the owner never sits and never lets anyone else pick a flower. The garden is wasted, and the owner is like a sickness that keeps it from doing any good. Valluvar says a stingy rich person is like that sickness for his own money.
university: The opening word edham (ஏதம், 'harm, fault, affliction, disease') is the predicate, and its subject is the man described in the rest of the couplet: thaan thuvvaan (தான் துவ்வான், 'he himself does not enjoy') and thakkaarkku ondru eedhal iyalbu ilaan (தக்கார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈதல் இயல்பு இலான், 'one who has no disposition to give even one thing to the worthy'). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar therefore read him as a disease (நோய்) to his own great wealth, as does Pope's explanation ('a disease to his wealth'); Solomon Pappaiah inverts it, making the wealth a disease in his keeping, and Sivayogi Sivakumar reads that he does harm to himself. The word iyalbu (இயல்பு, 'nature') stresses that the fault is temperamental, not circumstantial, and thakkaar (தக்கார், 'the deserving') narrows the duty of giving to worthy recipients, a classical criterion of proper gifts. Pope's verse rendering ('misery to men of churlish heart') follows the alternative sense. The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
அற்றார்க்கொன்று ஆற்றாதான் செல்வம் மிகநலம்
பெற்றாள் தமியள்மூத் தற்று.
transliteration:
Atraarkkondru Aatraadhaan Selvam Mikanalam
Petraal Thamiyalmooth Thatru
current_meaning: The riches of a person who gives nothing to the poor are like a very beautiful woman who grows old all alone.
elementary: Picture the most beautiful flower blooming inside a locked room where nobody ever sees it, until it slowly fades. Valluvar says money that never helps poor people is like that hidden flower: something lovely, wasted.
university: Atraar (அற்றார், 'those who have nothing, the destitute') are the intended recipients, and aatraadhaan (ஆற்றாதான்) is 'one who does not do (even one thing) for them'. The simile mika nalam petraaL thamiyaL mooththatru (மிக நலம் பெற்றாள் தமியள் மூத்தற்று) compares such wealth to 'a woman endowed with great beauty growing old alone'; Solomon Pappaiah and Pope's explanation specify 'without a husband', Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep 'alone'. The point of the comparison is waste: a good thing that exists to be shared lapses unused, the same logic as the chapter's poisonous-tree image in 1008 and its counterpart in Kural 216, where a generous man's wealth is a fruit tree in the middle of the village. The simile reflects the social world of classical Tamil literature, in which beauty fulfilled in married life is the norm; modern readers may note the period assumption while keeping the moral about unshared resources. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நச்சப் படாதவன் செல்வம் நடுவூருள்
நச்சு மரம்பழுத் தற்று.
transliteration:
Nachchap Pataadhavan Selvam Natuvoorul
Nachchu Marampazhuth Thatru
current_meaning: The riches of a person whom no one loves are like a poison tree bearing fruit in the middle of town.
elementary: Imagine a tree in the middle of the playground covered in shiny fruit, but the fruit is poisonous, so nobody can eat it. Valluvar says a selfish rich person's money is like that tree: right there in front of everyone, but no use to anyone.
university: The couplet is built on a pun: nachchap padaadhavan (நச்சப் படாதவன், 'one not loved', from நச்சு- 'to desire') and nachchu maram (நச்சு மரம், 'poison tree'). Pope's explanation identifies it as the etty tree (எட்டி, the nux-vomica, Strychnos nux-vomica), and Sivayogi Sivakumar quotes the proverb எட்டி பழுத்தால் என்ன, ஈயாதான் வாழ்ந்தால் என்ன ('what if the etty ripens, what if the non-giver prospers'). The setting naduvooruL (நடுவூருள், 'in the middle of the town') heightens the irony: the fruit is in full view and within reach of all, yet useless. Mu. Varadarasanar supplies the reason the man is unloved, that he helps no one. The image is the exact inverse of Kural 216, where the wealth of the generous is a fruit-bearing tree in the midst of the village, so Valluvar deliberately pairs the two chapters on Oppuravu and Nandriyil Selvam. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அன்பொரீஇத் தற்செற்று அறநோக்காது ஈட்டிய
ஒண்பொருள் கொள்வார் பிறர்.
transliteration:
Anporeeith Tharsetru Aranokkaadhu Eettiya
Onporul Kolvaar Pirar
current_meaning: Shining riches gathered by giving up love, starving yourself and ignoring what is right will be taken by others in the end.
elementary: A boy saves all his pocket money, never shares, never buys himself a treat, and even cheats a little to get more. One day he moves away and leaves the jar behind, and other kids spend it. Valluvar says money gathered in such a selfish, unhappy way ends up with someone else.
university: The couplet lists three things sacrificed in the getting: anbu oreei (அன்பு ஒரீஇ, 'having forsaken love', the -īi lengthening marking the verbal participle), thaR setRu (தற்செற்று, 'having afflicted oneself', i.e. denying oneself comfort), and aRam nokkaadhu (அறம் நோக்காது, 'without regard for virtue'). The resulting oNporuL (ஒண்பொருள், 'bright, glittering wealth') is taken by piRar (பிறர், 'others'). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Sivayogi Sivakumar read 'others will enjoy it', Kalaignar sharpens it to 'others will plunder it', and Pope's explanation has 'strangers will inherit'; Pope glosses the three omissions as friendship, comfort and charity. Pappaiah reads anbu as love shown to others through giving, which ties the couplet to the chapter's theme rather than to domestic affection. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
சீருடைச் செல்வர் சிறுதுனி மாரி
வறங்கூர்ந் தனையது உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Seerutaich Chelvar Sirudhuni Maari
Varangoorn Thanaiyadhu Utaiththu
current_meaning: When good rich people who are known for giving become poor for a short time, it is like a rain cloud that is empty for a while after giving its rain.
elementary: A rain cloud pours out all its water on the thirsty fields, and for a little while it looks thin and empty. But soon it fills up again. Valluvar says when kind, generous people run short for a while, it is just like that cloud: they gave a lot, and they will be full again.
university: After nine couplets on useless wealth, the chapter closes on its positive counterpart. Seerudaich chelvar (சீருடைச் செல்வர்) are 'rich men endowed with excellence', which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'famous' and Solomon Pappaiah 'famous for giving to others'. Their siRu thuni (சிறுதுனி) is 'a small distress', read by most commentators as a brief poverty; Pope renders 'brief poverty'. It is compared to maari vaRam koorndhanaiyadhu (மாரி வறங் கூர்ந்தனையது), 'like the rain cloud becoming impoverished', i.e. temporarily spent; Mu. Varadarasanar specifies 'the cloud that can protect the world'. The implication is that the generous man's want is temporary and itself a sign of his giving, as the cloud's emptiness follows its rain. Sivayogi Sivakumar takes a different line, reading the distress as the darkening that precedes rain and turns into good; Kalaignar reads the couplet as saying that even a shadow of poverty on such men is as grave as failed rain. The cloud image recalls Kural 211 on duty that expects no return, like the rain. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கருமத்தால் நாணுதல் நாணுந் திருநுதல்
நல்லவர் நாணுப் பிற.
transliteration:
Karumaththaal naanudhal naanum thirunudhal
nallavar naanup pira.
current_meaning: True shame is pulling back from a bad deed. Other kinds of shyness are just the natural modesty of lovely young women with bright foreheads.
elementary: Some kids feel shy when they have to sing in front of the class; that is one kind of shy. But Valluvar says the shame that really matters is the feeling that stops your hand just before you do something mean or wrong. That feeling is like a good friend inside you.
university: The chapter opens by defining its subject: naanudhal (நாணுதல், 'shrinking, being abashed') that arises karumaththaal (கருமத்தால், 'on account of a deed'), i.e. recoiling from a base act, is the naan (நாண்) of the good. Puliyur Kesikan, following the commentarial line of Parimelazhagar, glosses the second line as saying that the other shrinkings of mind, speech and body are the modesty proper to women of good family (thirunudhal nallavar, 'the good ones of beautiful brow'), so Valluvar separates a moral emotion open to everyone from a customary, gendered bashfulness. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it the same way, and Pope renders the moral sense as ‘generous shame’. Placed in the Kudiyiyal after Nanriyil Selvam (ch. 101) and before Kudiseyalvagai (ch. 103), the chapter treats naan as the inner guard of the well-born person. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh writes the same words; only spacing differs).

tamil:
ஊணுடை எச்சம் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல
நாணுடைமை மாந்தர் சிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Oonudai echcham uyirkkellaam veralla
naanudaimai maandhar sirappu.
current_meaning: Food, clothing and the other needs of life are the same for every living being. What makes good people special is a sense of shame.
elementary: A puppy eats, a bird sleeps, and you eat and sleep too. So what makes a person special? Valluvar says it is the little voice that says “that would be wrong, I'd be ashamed to do it.” Animals don't have that voice. People do.
university: Oon (ஊண், 'food'), udai (உடை, 'clothing') and echcham (எச்சம், 'the remainder', i.e. the other bodily needs) are veralla (வேறல்ல, 'not different') for all uyir (உயிர், 'living beings'). By contrast naanudaimai (நாணுடைமை, 'the possession of shame') is maandhar sirappu (மாந்தர் சிறப்பு, 'the distinction of humans'). Kesikan and Varadarasanar take the first line to cover all beings and sets of people. Pappaiah narrows the contrast: food and clothing are common to all people, while shame distinguishes the good. Kalaignar explains naanudaimai as avoiding what others condemn. The kural thus makes shame the defining mark of the human, an idea that echoes widely in Indian (Hitopadesha) and Greek (Protagoras) ethics. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஊனைக் குறித்த உயிரெல்லாம் நாண்என்னும்
நன்மை குறித்தது சால்பு.
transliteration:
Oonaik kuriththa uyirellaam naanennum
nanmai kuriththadhu saalpu.
current_meaning: Every living being lives in a body. In the same way, perfect character lives in the good quality called shame.
elementary: A snail lives in its shell and a turtle lives in its shell; they can't live without them. Valluvar says goodness lives inside shame the same way. If you take away a person's shame, their goodness has no home left.
university: The kural builds an exact parallel. Uyir ellaam oonaik kuriththa (உயிரெல்லாம் ஊனைக் குறித்த): all lives have the body of flesh (ஊன்) as their seat. Saalpu (சால்பு, 'fullness of noble character', the virtue treated in ch. 99, Saanraanmai) has as its seat the nanmai (நன்மை, 'goodness') called naan. The verb kuriththal ('to aim at, to take as one's place') is repeated in both lines. Kesikan presses the image further: as lives never willingly leave their body, saalpu never leaves shame. Kalaignar renders saalpu as maanbu ('dignity'). Pope's ‘perfect virtue ever dwells with shame’ keeps the doubled structure. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அணிஅன்றோ நாணுடைமை சான்றோர்க்கு அஃதின்றேல்
பிணிஅன்றோ பீடு நடை.
transliteration:
Aniandro naanudaimai saandrorkku ahdhindrel
piniandro peedu nadai.
current_meaning: Isn't a sense of shame the jewel of good people? Without it, isn't their proud walk just like a sickness?
elementary: Imagine a champion who wins a race and then struts around boasting and laughing at everyone else. It spoils everything, like a sickness. But a champion who wins and stays kind and modest shines like someone wearing a beautiful necklace. Modesty is that necklace.
university: Two rhetorical questions with ‘andro’ (அன்றோ, ‘is it not?’) frame the kural. Naanudaimai is ani (அணி, 'ornament, jewel') to the saandror (சான்றோர், 'the noble, the perfected'). Without it (ahdhu indrel), their peedu nadai (பீடு நடை, 'gait of eminence, proud bearing') is pini (பிணி, 'disease'). Varadarasanar reads the disease as the proud walk itself. Pappaiah, more pointedly, says it is a disease to those who must watch it. Kalaignar glosses naan here as inward remorse for a wrong done. Pope: ‘without it step of stately pride is piteous thing to see.’ Thirukkural.net prints a final full stop that ytamizh.com omits; the words are otherwise identical, so the difference is only punctuation.

tamil:
பிறர்பழியும் தம்பழியும் நாணுவார் நாணுக்கு
உறைபதி என்னும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Pirarpazhiyum thampazhiyum naanuvaar naanukku
uraipadhi ennum ulagu.
current_meaning: People who feel ashamed of other people's wrongs as much as their own are the ones the world calls the true home of shame.
elementary: When your friend gets caught being unkind, do you just laugh? Or do you feel a little hot in the face, as if it were you? Valluvar says the people who feel ashamed even when someone else does wrong are the ones whose hearts are truly good.
university: Pirar pazhi (பிறர்பழி, 'the blame or disgrace of others') and tham pazhi (தம்பழி, 'one's own disgrace') are set side by side. The one who naanuvaar (நாணுவார், 'feels shame') at both is called by the world naanukku uraipadhi (நாணுக்கு உறைபதி, 'the dwelling-place of shame itself'). Kesikan stresses that such a person weighs the two kinds of blame equally. Pappaiah reads ‘not only one's own but also others' blame’. Pope's couplet, ‘Who feel ashamed for others' guilt as for their own’, follows the same line. The kural extends shame from a private brake to a shared moral sensitivity, which fits the Kudiyiyal's concern with the honour of family and community. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நாண்வேலி கொள்ளாது மன்னோ வியன்ஞாலம்
பேணலர் மேலா யவர்.
transliteration:
Naanveli kollaadhu manno viyangnaalam
paenalar melaa yavar.
current_meaning: Great people would not want even the whole wide world if it meant losing shame, the fence that guards them.
elementary: A garden has a fence so goats can't come in and eat the flowers. Valluvar says good people keep a fence of shame around their hearts. Even if someone offered them the whole world, they wouldn't trade away that fence.
university: Naan veli (நாண்வேலி, 'the hedge or fence that is shame') is the central image. The melaayavar (மேலாயவர், 'the superior ones') will not paenal (பேணல், 'cherish, desire') the viyan gnaalam (வியன்ஞாலம், 'vast world') without taking (kollaadhu) that hedge; manno (மன்னோ) is an emphatic particle. Kesikan and Pappaiah, in the line of Parimelazhagar, take it to mean that the great choose shame rather than the wide world as their protection. Varadarasanar reads it as saying the great would not want to live in the wide world without the protecting hedge of shame. Pope gives a more poetic turn: ‘For men of lofty soul the earth's vast realms no charms retain’ unless the hedge stays intact. Sivayogi Sivakumar's modern reading, that one cannot rise to greatness without the hedge, is a minority interpretation. The text is identical on both sites.

tamil:
நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர் உயிர்ப்பொருட்டால்
நாண்துறவார் நாணாள் பவர்.
transliteration:
Naanaal uyiraith thurappar uyirpporuttaal
naanthuravaar naanaal pavar.
current_meaning: People who live by shame will give up their life to keep it, but they will never give up shame to save their life.
elementary: Some heroes in stories are asked to do something really wrong, like betray a friend, or else they'll be hurt. And they say no, even though it's scary. Valluvar says people with real shame would rather lose everything than do something shameful.
university: The kural is built as a chiasmus. Naanaal uyiraith thurappar (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர், 'for shame's sake they renounce life') is mirrored by uyir poruttaal naan thuravaar (உயிர்ப்பொருட்டால் நாண்துறவார், 'for life's sake they do not renounce shame'). Naan aalpavar (நாணாள்பவர், 'those who wield or rule by shame') are its subject. Kesikan frames it as a dilemma: when shame and life cannot both be kept, the noble let life go. Kalaignar substitutes maanam (honour), linking the kural to ch. 97 (Maanam), where similar sentiments appear (e.g. kural 969 on the yak that dies on losing its hair). Pope: ‘The men of modest soul for shame would life an offering make.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பிறர்நாணத் தக்கது தான்நாணா னாயின்
அறம்நாணத் தக்கது உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Pirarnaanath thakkadhu thaannaanaa naayin
aramnaanath thakkadhu udaiththu.
current_meaning: If a person feels no shame at things that would make others ashamed, then goodness itself (what is right) will be ashamed of that person.
elementary: Imagine someone does something so rude that everyone watching feels embarrassed, but he just grins. Valluvar says that even Goodness itself would feel embarrassed to be his friend and would quietly walk away from him.
university: The kural personifies aram (அறம், 'virtue, dharma'). If one does not feel shame (thaan naanaan aayin) at what is pirar naanath thakkadhu (பிறர்நாணத் தக்கது, 'fit to make others ashamed'), then he udaiththu (உடைத்து, 'has in him') something aram naanath thakkadhu, at which virtue itself would blush. There are two lines of interpretation. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar say virtue, ashamed, abandons him. Pappaiah and Kesikan say he harbours a fault at which virtue is ashamed. Kesikan's gloss reads the first line as ‘what onlookers would blame’. Pope's ‘Virtue will shrink away ashamed of thee!’ follows the abandonment reading. The repeated naanath thakkadhu across both lines is characteristic Valluvar wordplay. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
குலஞ்சுடும் கொள்கை பிழைப்பின் நலஞ்சுடும்
நாணின்மை நின்றக் கடை.
transliteration:
Kulanjudum kolgai pizhaippin nalanjudum
naaninmai nindrak kadai.
current_meaning: Slipping from good behaviour burns away the good name of your family. But once you become shameless, it burns away every good thing you have.
elementary: If you break a rule once, people might think less of your family for a while. But if you stop caring at all whether you do wrong, it's like a fire that keeps spreading and burns up everything good about you.
university: The kural ranks two fires with the same verb, sudum (சுடும், 'burns, destroys'). If kolgai (கொள்கை, 'one's settled conduct', glossed by the commentators as ozhukkam) pizhaippin (பிழைப்பின், 'should fail'), it burns the kulam (குலம், 'family, lineage'). But naaninmai (நாணின்மை, 'shamelessness') nindra kadai (நின்றக் கடை, 'once it becomes settled') burns all nalam (நலம், 'every good'). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read the second fire as more total than the first; Kesikan says the first ruins only the family's standing while the second consumes everything. Kalaignar connects the lines: failing to feel shame at one's lapse lets ruin spread. Pope: ‘'Twill race consume if right observance fail; 'Twill every good consume if shamelessness prevail.’ The text (with the doubled consonant in நின்றக் கடை) is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நாண்அகத் தில்லார் இயக்கம் மரப்பாவை
நாணால் உயிர்மருட்டி அற்று.
transliteration:
Naanagath thillaar iyakkam marappaavai
naanaal uyirmarutti atru.
current_meaning: The actions of people with no shame in their hearts are like a wooden puppet moved by strings, which only fools people into thinking it is alive.
elementary: Have you seen a puppet show? The puppet dances and waves, but it isn't really alive; someone is pulling strings. Valluvar says a person with no shame inside is like that: moving around, but with nothing real inside.
university: The chapter closes with a pun on naan (நாண்), which means both ‘shame’ and ‘cord, string’ (as in a bowstring). Those who lack naan agaththu (நாண் அகத்து, 'shame within') move like a marappaavai (மரப்பாவை, 'wooden doll, puppet') that, by naanaal (நாணால், 'by means of strings'), uyir maruttum (உயிர்மருட்டும், 'deceives people into thinking it has life'). Kesikan glosses the strings as the yantra cords of a mechanical doll, and Varadarasanar and Pappaiah describe a doll worked by rope to look alive. So the shameless are alive in appearance only, moved by outside pulls rather than by an inner moral life. The wordplay (shame in the first line, string in the second) is often singled out as one of Valluvar's finest. Pope: ‘'Tis as with strings a wooden puppet apes life's functions.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கருமம் செயஒருவன் கைதூவேன் என்னும்
பெருமையின் பீடுடையது இல்.
transliteration:
Karumam seya oruvan kaithooven ennum
perumaiyin peedudaiyadhu il.
current_meaning: There is no greater honour than a person's promise, 'I will not stop working to help my family grow.'
elementary: Imagine a girl who promises, ‘I will keep helping my family every day, and I won’t give up when it gets boring.’ Valluvar says that promise, kept day after day, is the proudest thing a person can wear, prouder than any medal.
university: The chapter opens by naming its ideal: the person who says kai thooven (கைதூவேன், ‘I will not let my hand rest’) in karumam (கருமம், ‘the work’), understood by Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan as the duty of raising one's kudi (குடி, ‘family, lineage, community’). Peedu (பீடு) means dignity or eminence, so the couplet ranks this self-imposed vow above every other form of perumai (பெருமை, ‘greatness’), the subject of chapter 98. Solomon Pappaiah widens kudi to ‘house and country’, a reading he keeps through the whole chapter, while Kesikan, in the commentarial line of Parimelazhagar, keeps it to one's own family line. Pope renders it ‘Who says “I’ll do my work, nor slack my hand”, / His greatness, clothed with dignity supreme, shall stand.’ The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஆள்வினையும் ஆன்ற அறிவும் எனஇரண்டின்
நீள்வினையால் நீளும் குடி.
transliteration:
Aalvinaiyum aandra arivum ena irandin
neelvinaiyaal neelum kudi.
current_meaning: A family grows and lasts through long, steady work that combines two things: hard effort and full knowledge.
elementary: Building a strong treehouse needs two things: strong arms to hammer and a smart plan so it doesn't fall. Valluvar says a family is the same: hard work plus good thinking, kept up for a long time, makes it grow tall.
university: The couplet names two instruments, aalvinai (ஆள்வினை, ‘manly exertion’, the theme of chapter 62) and aandra arivu (ஆன்ற அறிவு, ‘full, ripened knowledge’), and says that the neelvinai (நீள்வினை, ‘long, unbroken effort’) carried out with both makes the kudi neelum (நீளும், ‘lengthen, extend, flourish’). The play between neel- ‘long’ in the work and neel- ‘lengthen’ in the family is deliberate: duration in effort produces duration in the line. Pope captures this with ‘In deed prolonged, then lengthens out the race’s line.’ Kesikan and Varadarasanar both read the two as effort and knowledge joined in uninterrupted action; Karunanidhi adds ‘deep knowledge and perseverance.’ The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
குடிசெய்வல் என்னும் ஒருவற்குத் தெய்வம்
மடிதற்றுத் தான்முந் துறும்.
transliteration:
Kudiseyval ennum oruvarkuth theyvam
madidhatruth thaanmun thurum.
current_meaning: When a person decides, 'I will lift up my family,' even the gods tie up their clothes and hurry ahead to help.
elementary: Have you noticed that when you really decide to clean your room, things suddenly seem to fall into place? Valluvar says that when someone truly decides to lift up their family, it is as if heaven rolls up its sleeves and runs ahead to help.
university: The striking image is madi tharru (மடிதற்று, ‘having tucked up the fold of its garment’), the gesture of someone girding up to work or run, so that theyvam (தெய்வம்) mun urum (முந்துறும், ‘comes forward first’). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses theyvam as oozh (ஊழ், ‘destiny, fate’), keeping with the Kural's chapter 38; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as a deity tightening its garment; Karunanidhi, rationalising, calls it the force of nature known as divine action. Pope gives ‘With vest succinct the goddess leads the way.’ The verb kudiseyval (‘I will make my family’) is a first-person vow, continuing 1021. The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
சூழாமல் தானே முடிவெய்தும் தம்குடியைத்
தாழாது உஞற்று பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Soozhaamal thaane mudiveydhum thamkudiyaith
thaazhaadhu unjatru bavarkku.
current_meaning: For people who work hard without delay to lift up their family, the work gets done by itself, even before they have planned it.
elementary: When you practise piano every day without putting it off, one day a hard song just seems to play itself. Valluvar says that when people keep working for their family without delay, success often arrives before they even sit down to plan it.
university: Soozhaamal (சூழாமல், ‘without deliberating, without planning’) and thaane (தானே, ‘of itself’) frame the promise that the task mudiveydhum (முடிவெய்தும், ‘reaches completion’) for those who thaazhaadhu unjatrupavar (தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர், ‘strive without delay’). Kesikan, following the older commentary, attributes this to divine aid (தெய்வ உதவியால்), linking it to 1023; Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read it naturalistically, saying the capacity to finish comes to the prompt worker unsought. Karunanidhi has victories ‘pile up of themselves.’ Pope translates ‘Without a thought spontaneously, his end will gain.’ The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
குற்றம் இலனாய்க் குடிசெய்து வாழ்வானைச்
சுற்றமாச் சுற்றும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Kutram ilanaaik kudiseydhu vaazhvaanaich
sutramaach chutrum ulagu.
current_meaning: The world gathers around a person who lifts up their family without doing wrong, and treats them like one of its own family.
elementary: Think of a kind neighbour who works hard for her family and never cheats anyone. Soon the whole street treats her like family, bringing food and asking her advice. Valluvar says that is what happens to honest family-builders: everyone wants to be their relative.
university: Kutram ilanaai (குற்றம் இலனாய், ‘being without fault’) is the condition: the family must be raised by blameless means. The reward is a pun on sutram (சுற்றம், ‘kin, relatives’) and sutrum (சுற்றும், ‘surrounds, encircles’): the ulagu (உலகு, ‘world’) surrounds him as if it were his own relatives. Varadarasanar and Kesikan say people seek to become his kin; Pappaiah narrows ulagu to ‘the great’ (உயர்ந்தோர்), in keeping with the commentarial habit of reading ulagam as the worthy. Pope translates ‘The world shall circle him, and kindred claim.’ The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
நல்லாண்மை என்பது ஒருவற்குத் தான்பிறந்த
இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Nallaanmai enbadhu oruvarkuth thaanpirandha
illaanmai aakkik kolal.
current_meaning: True manliness means taking charge of and caring for the family you were born into.
elementary: Some people think being strong means winning fights. Valluvar says real strength is when you grow up and become the person your family can lean on, the one who takes care of things at home.
university: The couplet redefines nallaanmai (நல்லாண்மை, ‘good manliness, true valour’) by rhyming it with illaanmai (இல்லாண்மை, ‘mastery of the household’): real valour is aakkik kolal (ஆக்கிக் கொளல், ‘making one's own’) the governance of the home one was born in (thaan pirandha, தான் பிறந்த). Varadarasanar and Kesikan read it as taking on the ruling of one's birth-family; Pappaiah again extends it to house and country; Karunanidhi reverses the emphasis, saying the able ruler brings glory to the family of his birth. Pope gives ‘To him who gives his powers, the house from which he sprang to raise.’ The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
அமரகத்து வன்கண்ணர் போலத் தமரகத்தும்
ஆற்றுவார் மேற்றே பொறை.
transliteration:
Amaragaththu vankannar polath thamaragaththum
aatruvaar metre porai.
current_meaning: In battle, the heavy load falls on the brave. In the same way, in a family, the load falls on those who are able to carry it.
elementary: In a soccer game, the toughest players stand in front when the other team attacks. Valluvar says families are the same: when trouble comes, the strongest, most capable person has to step forward and carry the load.
university: The couplet balances amaragaththu (அமரகத்து, ‘in the battlefield’) against thamaragaththum (தமரகத்தும், ‘among one's own people too’); the vankannar (வன்கண்ணர், ‘the hard-eyed, the fearless’) of war correspond to the aatruvaar (ஆற்றுவார், ‘those who are able’) in the family, and on them falls porai (பொறை, ‘burden, load’). Varadarasanar stresses that though many are born into a family, the burden lies on the capable. Text note: ytamizh.com reads தமரகத்தும் (with the inclusive -um) while thirukkural.net prints தமரகத்து ஆற்றுவார்; the meaning is the same and this edition follows the -um reading, which Pope's ‘Amid his kindred so’ also reflects.

tamil:
குடிசெய்வார்க் கில்லை பருவம் மடிசெய்து
மானங் கருதக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Kudiseyvaark killai paruvam madiseydhu
maanang karudhak kedum.
current_meaning: People who work for their family cannot wait for the right time. If they are lazy or worry too much about their pride, the family falls apart.
elementary: If you wait for the ‘perfect day’ to do your chores, it never comes, and the mess just grows. Valluvar says people who care for a family can't wait for a perfect time or think a job is beneath them; they just have to get going.
university: Paruvam (பருவம், ‘season, proper time’) is denied to the kudiseyvaar (குடிசெய்வார், ‘those who make the family’): any time is the time. The second line names two enemies, madi (மடி, ‘sloth’, the theme of chapter 61) and maanam karudhal (மானம் கருதல், ‘considering one's pride or honour’), either of which makes the family kedum (கெடும், ‘perish’). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read maanam as standing on one's dignity, refusing humble work; Karunanidhi reads it as being shaken by insults directed at oneself. Pope gives ‘Wait for no season, when you would your house uprear; / ’Twill perish, if you wait supine, or hold your honour dear.’ The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
இடும்பைக்கே கொள்கலம் கொல்லோ குடும்பத்தைக்
குற்ற மறைப்பான் உடம்பு.
transliteration:
Idumbaikke kolkalam kollo kudumbaththaik
kutra maraippaan udambu.
current_meaning: Is the body of a person who protects their family from harm made only to hold suffering?
elementary: Think of a parent who works late, carries heavy bags, and gets up at night when the baby cries. Their body is tired and sore. Valluvar asks: is that body only made for hardship? His answer is that their toil is also full of love and worth.
university: The couplet is a rhetorical question: is the udambu (உடம்பு, ‘body’) of the one who kutram maraippaan (குற்றம் மறைப்பான், ‘wards off harm’ from his kudumbam, குடும்பம், ‘family’) merely an idumbaikke kolkalam (இடும்பைக்கே கொள்கலம், ‘a vessel for suffering alone’)? The particle kollo (கொல்லோ) marks wonder or doubt. Varadarasanar reads it plainly as ‘is his body only a home for suffering?’, conceding the hardship; Kesikan and Pappaiah draw the implied answer, that it is also a vessel of joy; Karunanidhi says such a person is honoured as one born to bear suffering. Pope gives ‘Is not his body vase that various sorrows fill, / Who would his household screen from every ill?’ The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
இடுக்கண்கால் கொன்றிட வீழும் அடுத்தூன்றும்
நல்லாள் இலாத குடி.
transliteration:
Idukkankaal kondrida veezhum aduththoondrum
nallaal ilaadha kudi.
current_meaning: A family with no good person to hold it up will fall, like a tree, when trouble cuts at its roots.
elementary: A young tree needs a stick tied beside it so the wind doesn't knock it over. Valluvar says a family is like that tree: when hard times blow, it needs a strong, caring person standing beside it, or it will fall.
university: The image is of a tree: idukkan (இடுக்கண், ‘misfortune’) strikes at its kaal (கால், ‘foot, base’) and kondrida (கொன்றிட, ‘cutting, killing’) brings it down, unless there is a nallaal (நல்லாள், ‘good person’) who aduththu oondrum (அடுத்து ஊன்றும், ‘stands close and props it up’). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah make the axe explicit (துன்பமாகிய கோடாரி, ‘the axe of misfortune’), and Kesikan names the tree; Pappaiah reads nallaal as ‘good children’. The couplet closes the chapter by turning 1021's vow into a warning about its absence. Pope gives ‘When trouble the foundation saps the house must fall, / If no strong hand be nigh to prop the tottering wall.’ The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
சுழன்றும்ஏர்ப் பின்னது உலகம் அதனால்
உழந்தும் உழவே தலை.
transliteration:
Suzhandrum-Erp pinnadhu ulagam adhanaal
uzhandhum uzhavae thalai.
current_meaning: The world turns to many kinds of work, but it still has to follow the plough. So even though it is hard, farming is the best of all jobs.
elementary: People can be bakers, builders, drivers or doctors, but every one of them still needs lunch, and lunch starts in a farmer's field. Farming is hard, sweaty work, yet Valluvar says it is the most important job of all, because every other job leans on it.
university: The chapter opens with its thesis: suzhandrum (சுழன்றும், 'though it whirls about', i.e. though people turn to many other callings) the world is Erp pinnadhu (ஏர்ப் பின்னது, 'behind the plough'), so uzhandhum (உழந்தும், 'even though it means toil') uzhavu is thalai (தலை, 'head, chief'). Puliyur Kesikan, in the commentarial line of Parimelazhagar, reads suzhandrum as people roaming through other trades because they see the hardship of farming, and the second line as a concession: farming is best despite that hardship; Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar agree. Uzhavu (ch. 104) stands in the Kudiyiyal section of Porutpal, between Kudiseyalvagai (ch. 103) and Nalkuravu (ch. 105, poverty), so Valluvar presents productive labour as the household's answer to want. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உழுவார் உலகத்தார்க்கு ஆணிஅஃ தாற்றாது
எழுவாரை எல்லாம் பொறுத்து.
transliteration:
Uzhuvaar ulagaththaarkku aaNi-aq thaatraadhu
ezhuvaarai ellaam poRuththu.
current_meaning: Farmers are like the pin that holds a wheel in place for the world, because they feed all the people who do not farm and do other work instead.
elementary: A wagon wheel has a small pin that holds it on the axle. Without that pin the wheel falls off and the whole cart stops. Valluvar says farmers are that pin: they feed everyone else, so the whole world keeps rolling because of them.
university: The image is the aaNi (ஆணி), the linchpin or axle-pin that keeps a cart's wheel in place; the ploughmen are the aaNi of ulagaththaar (உலகத்தார், 'the people of the world'). The second line gives the reason: aqthu aatraadhu ezhuvaarai ellaam poRuththu (அஃது ஆற்றாது எழுவாரை எல்லாம் பொறுத்து), 'bearing all who, unable to do that (ploughing), go off to other work'. Puliyur Kesikan, in the line of Parimelazhagar, glosses ezhuvaar as those who leave farming for other trades and are still fed by the farmers' grain; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it the same way, and Pope gives 'linch-pin of the world'. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; ytamizh hyphenates the transliteration aaNi-aq.

tamil:
உழுதுண்டு வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார்மற் றெல்லாம்
தொழுதுண்டு பின்செல் பவர்.
transliteration:
UzhudhuNdu vaazhvaarae vaazhvaarmaR Rellaam
thozhudhuNdu pinsel pavar.
current_meaning: Only those who live by farming and eating what they grow truly live. Everyone else bows to others for food and walks behind them.
elementary: Imagine growing your own tomatoes and eating them, compared with always having to ask someone else to share. Valluvar says the farmer who grows his own food can stand tall, while people who must keep asking others for food have to follow behind them.
university: The couplet sets uzhudhu uNdu (உழுது உண்டு, 'ploughing, eating') against thozhudhu uNdu (தொழுது உண்டு, 'bowing, eating'), a deliberate rhyme in which a single consonant separates self-reliance from servility. Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, glosses those who plough as urimai vaazhvinar (உரிமை வாழ்வினர், 'those who live by right'), and says the rest eat by paying court to others and pinsel (பின்செல், 'follow behind') them; Solomon Pappaiah adds that the farmer ploughs for others as well as for himself. The ideal is economic independence rather than caste or rank. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பலகுடை நீழலும் தங்குடைக்கீழ்க் காண்பர்
அலகுடை நீழ லவர்.
transliteration:
Palakudai neezhalum thangutaikkeezhk kaaNpar
alakutai neezha lavar.
current_meaning: Farmers whose fields are shaded by ripe grain will see many kings' umbrellas (signs of royal power) come under their own king's umbrella.
elementary: In old Tamil kingdoms a king's royal umbrella stood for his rule. Valluvar says that a land with plenty of grain becomes so strong and attractive that other lands come under its protection. Good farms make a strong country.
university: The couplet plays on kudai (குடை, the royal parasol, emblem of sovereignty) and neezhal (நீழல், 'shade'). alakudai neezhalavar (அலகுடை நீழலவர்) are those who have the shade of alaku (அலகு, ears of grain), that is, prosperous farmers; Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, glosses them as nel udaiyavar, 'owners of paddy', and also as karunaiyaalar, 'the compassionate', taking neezhal as the cool shade of grace (thannali), a reading Mu. Varadarasanar keeps. Such farmers 'see' the umbrellas of many kings come under their own king's umbrella, because grain surplus makes a realm strong. Solomon Pappaiah takes a softer line: people of other lands come to desire the farmers' ruler. Pope's 'Whose fields are shaded by the waving grain' brings out the pun. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; only word spacing differs.

tamil:
இரவார் இரப்பார்க்கொன்று ஈவர் கரவாது
கைசெய்தூண் மாலை யவர்.
transliteration:
Iravaar irappaarkkondru eevar karavaadhu
kaiseydhooN maalai yavar.
current_meaning: People who live by the work of their own hands never beg. They give to those who beg, without hiding what they have.
elementary: A girl who grows her own strawberries never has to ask anyone for strawberries. And when a friend asks for some, she shares happily instead of hiding the basket. Working with your own hands lets you be both proud and generous.
university: kai seydhu ooN maalaiyavar (கைசெய்து ஊண் மாலையவர்) means 'those whose nature (maalai, மாலை) is to eat by the work of their hands'. Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, identifies them with farmers (uzhavar) whose effort yields food. Two consequences follow: iravaar (இரவார், 'they do not beg') and they give irappaarkku ondru (இரப்பார்க்கு ஒன்று, 'something to those who beg') karavaadhu (கரவாது, 'without concealment'). Mu. Varadarasanar widens the subject to all who labour with their hands (thozhilaalar), while Solomon Pappaiah and Kesikan keep the focus on ploughing. The couplet also looks ahead to the later chapters Iravu (106) and Iravachcham (107) on begging. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உழவினார் கைம்மடங்கின் இல்லை விழைவதூஉம்
விட்டேம்என் பார்க்கும் நிலை.
transliteration:
Uzhavinaar kaimmadangin illai vizhaivadhooum
vittaemen paarkkum nilai.
current_meaning: If farmers stop working, even people who say, 'We have given up all our desires,' cannot keep living their way of life.
elementary: Even people who have given up toys, money and fancy things to live a simple, holy life still need a bowl of rice each day. If farmers stopped working, those holy people would go hungry too. So everyone, even a saint, depends on the farmer.
university: uzhavinaar kai madangin (உழவினார் கை மடங்கின்) means 'if the ploughmen's hands fold (stop working)'. Then illai ... nilai (இல்லை ... நிலை): there is no standing even for those who say vizhaivadhooum vittaem (விழைவதூஉம் விட்டேம், 'we have renounced even what is desired'), that is, the ascetics (thuRavigaL). Puliyur Kesikan, in Parimelazhagar's line, takes vizhaivadhu as the food everyone desires and reads nilai as the renunciant's steadiness in his dharma; Solomon Pappaiah agrees, and Kalaignar says even renouncers must look to the farmer's hand. The couplet links back to the Aram section's chapter on ascetics (Neeththaar Perumai, ch. 3) and to rain as the support of austerity (Kural 19), placing the household economy beneath the renunciant. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the alapedai lengthening -ooum is printed in both.

tamil:
தொடிப்புழுதி கஃசா உணக்கின் பிடித்தெருவும்
வேண்டாது சாலப் படும்.
transliteration:
Thotippuzhudhi kaqsaa uNakkin pitiththeruvum
vaeNtaadhu saalap padum.
current_meaning: If ploughed soil is dried until one measure shrinks to a quarter, the crop will grow richly without even a handful of manure.
elementary: If you dig a garden, break up the lumps and let the sun dry the soil really well, the plants grow strong even without extra fertiliser. Getting the ground ready carefully is half the work of farming.
university: This is one of the Kural's most technical couplets. thodi (தொடி) and kaqsu (கஃசு) are weights: one palam and a quarter palam. thodippuzhudhi kaqsaa uNakkin (தொடிப்புழுதி கஃசா உணக்கின்) means 'if you dry a palam of ploughed dust down to a quarter-palam', that is, plough repeatedly and sun-dry the soil until three-quarters of its moisture weight is lost. Then piditheruvum vaeNdaadhu (பிடித்து எருவும் வேண்டாது, 'not needing even a fistful of manure') the crop saalap padum (சாலப் படும், 'will flourish greatly'). Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar give this measure-based reading, following Parimelazhagar; Solomon Pappaiah converts it to about 35 grams reduced to 8.75 grams, and Kalaignar stresses repeated ploughing. Pope keeps the weights as 'ounce' and 'quarter-ounce'. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஏரினும் நன்றால் எருவிடுதல் கட்டபின்
நீரினும் நன்றதன் காப்பு.
transliteration:
Erinum nandraal eruvidudhal kattapin
neerinum nandradhan kaappu.
current_meaning: Adding manure is better than ploughing. After weeding, guarding the crop is even better than watering it.
elementary: Planting a garden is not the end of the job. You feed the soil, pull out the weeds, and then you have to protect the plants from birds, goats and trampling feet. Watching over what you grew matters even more than watering it.
university: The couplet ranks the farmer's tasks: eruviduthal (எருவிடுதல், 'applying manure') is better than Er (ஏர், 'ploughing'), and after katta (கட்ட, 'weeding'; Kesikan and Varadarasanar gloss kattapin as 'after removing weeds') kaappu (காப்பு, 'guarding, protection') is better than neer (நீர், 'watering'). Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, reads the sequence as plough, manure, weed, water, guard, with each later step more decisive than the one before it; Kalaignar's paraphrase ranks weeding and watering as 'very good' and protection as best. The point is that the work ends with vigilant protection of what has been produced, a principle the Porutpal applies to wealth as well as crops. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
செல்லான் கிழவன் இருப்பின் நிலம்புலந்து
இல்லாளின் ஊடி விடும்.
transliteration:
Sellaan kizhavan iruppin nilampulandhu
illaaLin ooti vidum.
current_meaning: If the owner does not go to his land and look after it, the land will sulk and turn away from him, like an upset wife.
elementary: If you plant a garden and then forget about it, the plants droop and the weeds take over, as if the garden were upset with you. Valluvar says land is like a family member: it needs you to show up and care for it every day.
university: kizhavan (கிழவன்) here means 'owner' (of the land), not 'old man'; sellaan iruppin (செல்லான் இருப்பின்) means 'if he stays without going (to the field)'. The land then pulandhu (புலந்து, 'feeling aggrieved') and oodi vidum (ஊடி விடும், 'turns away in sulking') like an illaaL (இல்லாள், 'wife'). The verbs pulavi and oodal are technical terms of the Kamaththuppal for a lover's quarrel (compare chapters 131-133), so Valluvar borrows the vocabulary of love to describe neglected land. Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, glosses that the owner must go daily and do what is needed; Solomon Pappaiah spells out that the land, like a wife, first withers inwardly and then withholds its yield. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இலமென்று அசைஇ இருப்பாரைக் காணின்
நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்.
transliteration:
Ilamendru asaii iruppaaraik kaaNin
nilamennum nallaaL nakum.
current_meaning: When the good lady called Earth sees people sitting lazily and saying, 'We are poor,' she laughs at them.
elementary: Imagine someone sitting beside a big empty field and complaining, 'I have nothing to eat!' Valluvar says the Earth would giggle, because the field is right there, ready to grow food for anyone willing to work it.
university: ilam endru (இலம் என்று, 'saying "we have nothing"') and asaii iruppaar (அசைஇ இருப்பார், 'those who sit idle', with asaii lengthened by alapedai) are the people the Earth laughs at. nilam ennum nallaaL (நிலம் என்னும் நல்லாள்) means 'the good woman called Earth', and nakum (நகும்) means 'will laugh'. Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, says she laughs to herself, because the remedy for their poverty lies in her and needs only effort; Solomon Pappaiah reads the laughter as mockery, and Kalaignar names her Bhoomiththaai (Mother Earth). The chapter ends where it began, with land as the answer to want, and leads directly into Nalkuravu (ch. 105, Poverty). Pope's rendering is 'The earth, that kindly dame, will laugh to see, / Men seated idle pleading poverty.' The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இன்மையின் இன்னாதது யாதெனின் இன்மையின்
இன்மையே இன்னா தது.
transliteration:
Inmaiyin innaadhadhu yaadhenin inmaiyin
inmaiyae innaa thadhu.
current_meaning: If you ask what hurts more than being poor, the only answer is being poor itself. Nothing else hurts as much.
elementary: Imagine someone asking, “What hurts more than a really bad toothache?” and the answer is, “Only a really bad toothache.” Valluvar says being so poor that you have nothing is like that: there is nothing else to compare it with, because it is the worst hurt of its kind.
university: The chapter opens with a deliberately circular definition built on repetition of inmai (இன்மை, ‘not-having, want’): inmaiyin innaadhadhu (‘what is more grievous than want’) is answered by inmaiyae (‘want itself’). Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar both gloss inmaiyin as a comparative (‘like poverty’), so the sense is that poverty is its own only standard of comparison; Kalaignar makes the same point by saying no other sorrow can serve as an upamai (simile) for it. The figure is a classic Tamil ananvaya-like device in which the subject is compared to itself to mark it as incomparable, and Pope’s ‘Nothing pains more than poverty, save poverty alone’ preserves the tautology. Nalkuravu (நல்குரவு) in the chapter title is the standard classical word for destitution; placed in the Kudiyiyal right after Uzhavu (ch. 104, agriculture, the remedy for want) and before Iravu (ch. 106, begging), the chapter traces the social consequences of losing one’s means. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net apart from spacing.

tamil:
இன்மை எனவொரு பாவி மறுமையும்
இம்மையும் இன்றி வரும்.
transliteration:
Inmai enavoru paavi maRumaiyum
immaiyum indri varum.
current_meaning: The evil thing called poverty, when it comes, takes away a person's happiness in this life and in the next life too.
elementary: Think of a villain in a story who sneaks in and takes away both your lunch today and your treat for tomorrow. Valluvar calls poverty a villain like that: it takes away the good things you could enjoy now, and also the good you could do for others, which helps you later.
university: Valluvar personifies inmai as oru paavi (ஒரு பாவி), ‘a sinner, a wicked one’, a vivid figure for an abstract condition. The second line says it comes so that maRumai (மறுமை, the next world) and immai (இம்மை, this world) are both lost. Solomon Pappaiah spells out the logic the commentators share: the poor cannot give to others, so they lose the merit that secures the next world, and they have nothing to enjoy themselves, so they lose this world too; Puliyur Kesikan likewise speaks of losing worldly pleasure here and the bliss of heaven hereafter. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads the pair temporally (present and future), and Kalaignar secularises it as loss of peace now and later. The Kural thus ties wealth to aram (virtue) through the duty of giving, a link developed in the Arathuppaal chapters on Eekai (giving) and Oppuravu (helpfulness). The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும் தொகையாக
நல்குரவு என்னும் நசை.
transliteration:
Tholvaravum thoalum kedukkum thogaiyaaga
nalkuravu ennum nasai.
current_meaning: The hungry want called poverty destroys, all at once, a family's long history and its good name.
elementary: Imagine a family that has been known for generations as kind and honest. If someone in it becomes so desperate that wanting things takes over, they might do things that spoil the family’s good name all at once, like one spill ruining a whole painting.
university: The key word is nasai (நசை, ‘desire, craving’): Valluvar does not just say nalkuravu but ‘nalkuravu ennum nasai’, the craving that is called poverty, suggesting that destitution shows itself as a gnawing want. Tholvaravu (தொல்வரவு) is ‘what has come down from of old’, the dignity or heritage of one’s line, and thoal (தோல்) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan as pugazh (fame, honour); the English explanation carried on ytamizh.com renders it ‘the dignity of one’s speech’, reflecting an older reading that associates thoal with elevated, well-formed words. Thogaiyaaga (‘all together, at a stroke’) stresses the suddenness of the ruin. Kalaignar shifts the causation slightly, saying that poverty breeds greed which then ruins lineage and fame. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும் இன்மை இளிவந்த
சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு தரும்.
transliteration:
IRpiRandhaar kaNNaeyum inmai iLivandha
soRpiRakkum soarvu tharum.
current_meaning: Poverty makes even people from good families so tired and weak that low, shameful words come out of their mouths.
elementary: When you are very tired and hungry, you might snap at someone even though you are usually polite. Valluvar says being very poor can make even well-brought-up people so worn down that unkind or embarrassing words slip out.
university: IRpiRandhaar (இற்பிறந்தார்) are ‘those born in a (good) house’, i.e. of noble family, and the -um of kaNNaeyum (‘even in them’) concedes that breeding is no protection. Inmai gives soarvu (சோர்வு, ‘slackness, exhaustion, lapse of vigilance’) from which iLivandha sol (இளிவந்த சொல், ‘words that bring disgrace’) is born. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it this way: poverty causes the lapse, and the lapse produces demeaning speech. Puliyur Kesikan, notably, reverses the causation, saying that the slackness which leads to base acts is itself what brings poverty even to good families, a reading that turns the couplet into a warning rather than a lament. Pope’s ‘Oblivion that gives birth to words that bring disgrace’ takes soarvu as forgetfulness of one’s station. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நல்குரவு என்னும் இடும்பையுள் பல்குரைத்
துன்பங்கள் சென்று படும்.
transliteration:
Nalkuravu ennum idumbaiyuL palkuraith
thunbangaL sendru padum.
current_meaning: Inside the one trouble called poverty, many kinds of sorrows gather and settle.
elementary: Have you seen one leak in a roof let in rain that ruins the carpet, the books and the bed? Valluvar says poverty is like that one leak: many other troubles come pouring in through it.
university: Idumbai (இடும்பை, ‘affliction, distress’) names poverty as one trouble, and palkurai (பல்குரை, ‘of many kinds’) thunbangaL (‘sorrows’) are said to ‘go and settle’ (sendru padum) within it. Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah read this as all sorrows being contained in poverty, so that poverty is the sum of misfortunes; Mu. Varadarasanar says they ‘arise and grow’ inside it; Kalaignar reverses the image slightly, with many sorrows springing out of poverty. Either way poverty is the matrix of other ills, which prepares for the later couplets on lost respect (1046), estranged kin (1047) and sleepless dread (1048-1049). Pope’s ‘Attendant sorrows plenteous grow’ follows the ‘springing up’ reading. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நற்பொருள் நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லினும் நல்கூர்ந்தார்
சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்.
transliteration:
NaRporuL nangunarndhu sollinum nalkoorndhaar
soRporuL soarvu padum.
current_meaning: Even when poor people speak true and wise things that they fully understand, their words are ignored and come to nothing.
elementary: Imagine two children giving the same right answer in class, but everyone only listens to the one with the fancy new shoes. Valluvar noticed that people often ignore what poor people say, even when it is wise, and that this is unfair.
university: NaRporuL (நற்பொருள்) is ‘good matter’, which Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar specify as the sense of good books (nool), and nangunarndhu (‘having understood well’) stresses that the speaker is genuinely learned. Yet the soRporuL (சொற்பொருள், ‘the meaning of the words’) of nalkoorndhaar (நல்கூர்ந்தார், ‘those who have become poor’) suffers soarvu, here ‘failure, lapse’: it is not heard or heeded. The same word soarvu that meant inner weariness in 1044 here describes the social fate of the poor man’s speech, a deliberate echo. Solomon Pappaiah puts it simply: if the speaker is poor, his words are not honoured. Pope’s ‘Their sense from memory of mankind will fade away’ takes the lapse as being forgotten. The observation is descriptive and critical, not an endorsement of the bias. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு ஈன்றதா யானும்
பிறன்போல நோக்கப் படும்.
transliteration:
ARanjaaraa nalkuravu eendradhaa yaanum
piRanpoala noakkap padum.
current_meaning: A person in poverty that has no goodness about it is looked at like a stranger, even by the mother who gave birth to them.
elementary: A mother’s love is the strongest love there is. Valluvar warns that if someone becomes poor because of bad choices and also turns away from doing right, people may turn away from him, and even his own family may feel hurt and distant.
university: The decisive qualifier is aRanjaaraa (அறஞ்சாரா, ‘not joined to aram, virtue’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it as ‘poverty not in keeping with virtue’, i.e. destitution that is unrighteous in cause or accompaniment; Solomon Pappaiah glosses it as poverty without just reasons; Kalaignar makes it moral, the person who abandons virtue because of poverty. Eendra thaai (ஈன்ற தாய், ‘the mother who bore him’) is the strongest possible bond, and piRan poala (‘like another, a stranger’) marks its collapse. Read with the qualifier, the couplet does not say that every poor person is rejected, only that want combined with the loss of aram estranges even the closest kin. The ytamizh.com English explanation (‘reduced to absolute poverty’) passes over aRanjaaraa, a reminder that translations differ on how much moral weight to give it. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இன்றும் வருவது கொல்லோ நெருநலும்
கொன்றது போலும் நிரப்பு.
transliteration:
Indrum varuvadhu kolloa nerunalum
kondradhu poalum nirappu.
current_meaning: A poor person asks in fear, 'Will the need that almost killed me yesterday come again today?'
elementary: Imagine having a very scary day, and waking up the next morning worried: “Will it happen again today?” Valluvar says a very poor person feels like that every single day, afraid that yesterday’s hunger and worry will come back.
university: The couplet is spoken in the voice of the poor man himself, an unusual dramatic touch in the Porutpaal. Nirappu (நிரப்பு, ‘want, need’) is a synonym of nalkuravu, and the particle kolloa (கொல்லோ) marks anxious questioning: ‘will it come today too?’. Nerunal (நெருநல், ‘yesterday’) and kondradhu poalum (‘as though it killed’) describe the daily ordeal as a near-death; Puliyur Kesikan adds the implied cry ‘if it comes, what shall I do?’, while Mu. Varadarasanar frames it as the poor man’s daily trembling. Kalaignar reads it as a longing that it may not return. The present-tense dread contrasts with the general statements of the earlier couplets and leads into the sleeplessness of 1049. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நெருப்பினுள் துஞ்சலும் ஆகும் நிரப்பினுள்
யாதொன்றும் கண்பாடு அரிது.
transliteration:
NeruppinuL thunjalum aagum nirappinuL
yaadhondrum kaNpaadu aridhu.
current_meaning: A person might somehow sleep in the middle of a fire, but in the middle of poverty, they cannot close their eyes at all.
elementary: Have you ever been so worried that you could not fall asleep? Valluvar says that worrying about having no food or money is so strong that it is even harder to sleep than if you were lying next to a fire.
university: The hyperbole sets two ‘insides’ side by side: neruppinuL (‘within fire’) and nirappinuL (‘within want’).
