Thunjal (துஞ்சல், ‘sleeping’) is said to be possible (aagum) in the first, while kaNpaadu (கண்பாடு, ‘the closing of the eyes, sleep’) is aridhu (‘rare, hard’) in the second, yaadhondrum (‘by any means at all’). Puliyur Kesikan explains how sleeping in fire might be possible, through the help of mantra and medicine, and Solomon Pappaiah through yogic power; Pappaiah also narrows nirappu to the torment of hunger. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep the image general. The couplet follows naturally from 1048: the dread of tomorrow’s want is what keeps the poor awake. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
துப்புர வில்லார் துவரத் துறவாமை
உப்பிற்கும் காடிக்கும் கூற்று.
transliteration:
Thuppura villaar thuvarath thuRavaamai
uppiRkum kaadikkum koottru.
current_meaning: When very poor people do not give up worldly life completely, they only become death to other people's salt and rice-water, eating up what others have.
elementary: Imagine someone who has nothing and keeps taking a little salt and soup from the neighbours, but does nothing else with his life. Valluvar says that person should either change his life completely or choose a simple life of giving things up, instead of just using up what others need.
university: Thuppuravu (துப்புரவு) means the things one enjoys or lives by, so thuppuravillaar are ‘those without any means’. Thuvara (‘completely’) thuRavaamai (‘not renouncing’) is the fault named: Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar say the only course left to such people is full renunciation, and failing it they are merely koottru (கூற்று, Yama, death) to uppu (salt) and kaadi (காடி, sour rice-water or gruel; Pope’s ‘vinegar’). Solomon Pappaiah sharpens the social point: by staying in household life they consume the salt and gruel in other people’s homes. Kalaignar reads thuppuravu as orderliness, so the subject becomes those impoverished by disorderly living. The chapter thus ends by pointing toward thuRavu (renunciation), linking the Porutpaal back to the Thuravaraviyal of the first book, and leads into Iravu (begging) in ch. 106. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இரக்க இரத்தக்கார்க் காணின் கரப்பின்
அவர்பழி தம்பழி அன்று.
transliteration:
Irakka iraththakkaark kaanin karappin
avarpazhi thampazhi andru.
current_meaning: If you meet people who are right to ask, you may ask them for help. If they hide what they have and say no, the blame is theirs, not yours.
elementary: Imagine you are really hungry and you politely ask a kind neighbour who has plenty of food for a little. If that neighbour pretends to have nothing, you did nothing wrong by asking. The person who hid the food is the one who acted badly.
university: The chapter on iravu (இரவு, 'asking, mendicancy') follows Nalkuravu (ch. 105, poverty) and is balanced by Iravachcham (ch. 107, dread of begging); together they permit asking only in real need and only of fitting givers. The key word irakka iraththakkaar (இரத்தக்கார், 'those of whom it is fit to ask') limits the permission: one may ask those able and willing to give. Karappin (கரப்பின், 'if they conceal') names the vice of hiding what one has, a word the chapter returns to again and again (karappu, karaththal); the commentarial line that follows Parimelazhagar, as reflected in Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan, takes the blame (pazhi) as falling wholly on the one who conceals. Pope renders it 'Theirs is the sin, not yours, if they the gift deny.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இன்பம் ஒருவற்கு இரத்தல் இரந்தவை
துன்பம் உறாஅ வரின்.
transliteration:
Inbam oruvarku iraththal irandhavai
thunbam uraaa varin.
current_meaning: Even asking for help can be a pleasure, if what you ask for comes to you without pain for either person.
elementary: If you ask a friend to share a crayon and they hand it over with a smile, asking feels nice, not embarrassing. Asking only hurts when the other person sighs or makes you feel small.
university: Valluvar makes the surprising claim that iraththal (இரத்தல், 'begging') can itself be inbam (இன்பம், 'pleasure'), on one condition: that what is begged comes thunbam uraaa (துன்பம் உறாஅ, 'without suffering'), where the lengthened uraaa is an alapedai (metrical lengthening). Commentators differ on whose suffering is meant: Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as the asker's (the gift comes without hardship), Solomon Pappaiah as the giver's reluctance, and Kalaignar as both minds, giver's and receiver's, being free of pain. The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar stresses that the pleasure depends on the giver's goodwill (Puliyur Kesikan: ஈவாரது நல்லுணர்வால்). Pope: 'Even to ask an alms may pleasure give, / If what you ask without annoyance you receive.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கரப்பிலா நெஞ்சின் கடனறிவார் முன்நின்று
இரப்புமோ ரேஎர் உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Karappilaa nenjin kadanarivaar munnindru
irappumor eer udaiththu.
current_meaning: Asking can even have a kind of beauty, when you stand before people who hide nothing in their hearts and know what they should do.
elementary: Asking your grandmother, who loves to share, for a slice of cake doesn't feel bad at all. It can even feel nice, because she is happy you asked.
university: Karappilaa nenju (கரப்பிலா நெஞ்சு, 'a heart without concealment') and kadan arivaar (கடனறிவார், 'those who know their duty') describe the ideal giver. Kadan is read as duty (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah: 'this is my duty'), while Puliyur Kesikan glosses the givers as people who understand honour (மானம் அறிபவர்). The striking word is eer (ஏஎர், with alapedai lengthening, 'beauty, grace'): standing before such givers, even begging has beauty. The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar reads the -um in irappum ('even begging') as conceding that begging is normally without grace. Pope: 'To stand as suppliants affords especial grace.' Texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree, both printing the sandhi form இரப்புமோ ரேஎர்.

tamil:
இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும் கரத்தல்
கனவிலும் தேற்றாதார் மாட்டு.
transliteration:
Iraththalum eedhale polum karaththal
kanavilum thetraadhaar maattu.
current_meaning: Asking people who would never hold back, not even in a dream, is as worthy of respect as giving.
elementary: Some people love sharing so much that when you ask them, it's like you're doing them a favour. With friends like that, asking feels almost as good as giving.
university: The line iraththalum eedhale polum (இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும், 'begging too is just like giving') is one of the boldest claims in the Kural, and the emphatic ē in eedhale strengthens the equation. Its condition is that the giver karaththal kanavilum thetraadhaar (கரத்தல் கனவிலும் தேற்றாதார், 'does not know concealment even in a dream'). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it as conferring the same dignity (சிறப்பு, பெருமை) on such asking as on giving. The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar explains the equation by the giver's joy: asking such a person gives him the chance to give. Pope: 'To beg of such ... is in fact the same as giving.' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

tamil:
கரப்பிலார் வையகத்து உண்மையால் கண்ணின்று
இரப்பவர் மேற்கொள் வது.
transliteration:
Karappilaar vaiyagaththu unmaiyaal kannindru
irappavar merkol vadhu.
current_meaning: Some people are willing to stand before others and ask for help only because the world has people who never hold back when asked.
elementary: People bring their empty buckets to a well because they know the well has water. In the same way, people in need ask because they know there are kind people who will share.
university: The kural explains why anyone begs at all: because karappilaar (கரப்பிலார், 'those without concealment') exist in the world (vaiyagaththu unmaiyaal). Kan nindru (கண்ணின்று, 'standing before the eyes') is read in two ways: Mu. Varadarasanar takes it as standing in front of a giver, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as asking with the eyes rather than with words, the silent request of the proud poor. Puliyur Kesikan adds that such people beg only to preserve life. The sense of merkolvadhu (மேற்கொள்வது, 'taking up' a practice) suggests begging chosen reluctantly because generous givers are known to exist. The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree (மேற்கொள் வது with a space in both).

tamil:
கரப்பிடும்பை யில்லாரைக் காணின் நிரப்பிடும்பை
எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு கெடும்.
transliteration:
Karappidumbai yillaaraik kaanin nirappidumbai
ellaam orungu kedum.
current_meaning: Just seeing people who never hide what they have is enough to make all the pains of being poor go away at once.
elementary: When a hungry child sees a kind lunch lady who always shares, the worry disappears right away. Just seeing someone generous makes the scary feeling go.
university: The kural plays on two compounds built on idumbai (இடும்பை, 'affliction'): karappidumbai, the affliction (or 'disease', in Pappaiah's gloss நோய்) of concealment that belongs to the miser, and nirappidumbai, the affliction of want that belongs to the poor. The miser's karappu is thus treated as a sickness of its own, the counterpart of the beggar's poverty. Kaanin (காணின், 'if one but sees') shows that the mere sight of such a giver ends ellaam orungu (எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு, 'all together') the beggar's distress. Puliyur Kesikan adds that this holds for one who begs without losing self-respect (மானம் விடாமல்), and Kalaignar calls concealment an இழிநிலை (base state). The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree, both printing the sandhi form யில்லாரைக்.

tamil:
இகழ்ந்தெள்ளாது ஈவாரைக் காணின் மகிழ்ந்துள்ளம்
உள்ளுள் உவப்பது உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Igazhndhellaadhu eevaaraik kaanin magizhndhullam
ullul uvappadhu udaiththu.
current_meaning: When someone who asks meets givers who give without looking down on them or mocking them, their heart is filled with deep joy.
elementary: If you ask for help and the person helps you with a kind smile instead of laughing at you, you feel warm and happy inside. How we give matters as much as what we give.
university: Igazhndhu ellaadhu (இகழ்ந்து எள்ளாது, 'without despising, without mocking') names the two insults a giver can add to a gift, contempt and derision; Pappaiah glosses them as அவமதிக்காமல், இழிவாகப் பேசாமல். The response is doubled for emphasis: magizhndhu (மகிழ்ந்து, 'rejoicing') and ullul uvappadhu (உள்ளுள் உவப்பது, 'delighting within the innermost heart'). The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar places the joy in the asker, and the next chapter, Iravachcham, will show the opposite case, where contempt makes asking unbearable. Pope: 'The minds of askers, through and through, will thrill with joy.' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

tamil:
இரப்பாரை இல்லாயின் ஈர்ங்கண்மா ஞாலம்
மரப்பாவை சென்றுவந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Irappaarai illaayin eerngkanmaa nyaalam
marappaavai sendruvan thatru.
current_meaning: If there were no people who ask for help, all the coming and going in this cool, wide world would be like wooden puppets moving back and forth.
elementary: Imagine a toy theatre where wooden puppets bounce around on strings. They move, but they don't really care about anything. Valluvar says that if no one ever needed help, people would be like those puppets, busy but with no kindness to show.
university: Eerngkanmaa nyaalam (ஈர்ங்கண்மா ஞாலம், 'the cool, wide, great earth') and marappaavai (மரப்பாவை, 'wooden doll') give the image: Mu. Varadarasanar explains it as a wooden puppet moved by strings, so that human activity without askers would be mechanical motion without inner meaning. The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar takes the point to be that giving is what gives life its moral content, and giving needs askers. Kalaignar reads the couplet differently, making those who keep the poor at a distance no different from operated puppets. Pope: 'The mighty earth ... Will be a stage where wooden puppets come and go.' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree (சென்றுவந் தற்று in both).

tamil:
ஈவார்கண் என்னுண்டாம் தோற்றம் இரந்துகோள்
மேவார் இலாஅக் கடை.
transliteration:
Eevaarkan ennundaam thotram irandhukol
mevaar ilaaak kadai.
current_meaning: If no one wanted to ask and receive, what fame or honor could givers ever have?
elementary: A goalkeeper can only be a hero if someone kicks the ball. In the same way, a generous person can only shine if someone needs their help.
university: Thotram (தோற்றம், 'appearance, eminence') is glossed as pugazh (புகழ், 'fame') by Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar. Irandhu kol mevaar (இரந்துகோள் மேவார், 'those who wish to take by asking') are the counterpart without whom the giver's eminence cannot exist; ilaaak kadai has the alapedai lengthening ilaaa. Read with 1058, the couplet pair makes askers necessary to the moral economy of giving, a theme going back to Ch. 23 (Eegai) and Ch. 24 (Pugazh), where fame is linked to giving. Pope: 'What glory will there be to men of generous soul, / When none are found to love the askers' role?' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

tamil:
இரப்பான் வெகுளாமை வேண்டும் நிரப்பிடும்பை
தானேயும் சாலும் கரி.
transliteration:
Irappaan vegulaamai vendum nirappidumbai
thaaneyum saalum kari.
current_meaning: A person who asks should not get angry when refused. The pain of their own need is proof enough of how things stand.
elementary: If you ask a friend to share and they say no, don't get mad. You know how it feels not to have enough, so maybe they don't have enough either, or maybe it just wasn't the right time.
university: Vegulaamai (வெகுளாமை, 'not becoming angry') recalls Chapter 31 (Vegulaamai), here applied to the one who is refused. The second line is read in more than one way: nirappidumbai thaaneyum saalum kari (நிரப்பிடும்பை தானேயும் சாலும் கரி) can mean that the asker's own poverty is sufficient witness (kari, கரி) that things are not always available when wanted (Puliyur Kesikan, Pappaiah), that the asker's poverty teaches him (Mu. Varadarasanar), or that the refuser may be in the same plight as himself (Kalaignar). The commentarial tradition following Parimelazhagar takes the beggar's own want as reason enough for patience toward a refusal. Pope: 'Askers refused from wrath must stand aloof; / The plague of poverty itself is ample proof.' The texts on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

tamil:
கரவாது உவந்தீயும் கண்ணன்னார் கண்ணும்
இரவாமை கோடி உறும்.
transliteration:
Karavaadhu uvandheeyum kannannaar kannum
iravaamai koadi urum.
current_meaning: Even when there are people as dear as your own eyes who would gladly give without hiding anything, never asking them at all is worth ten million times more.
elementary: Imagine your kindest aunt would happily give you anything you asked for. The Kural says it is still far better, and makes you stronger, to manage on your own and not ask, even from someone that kind.
university: The chapter Iravaccham (இரவச்சம், 'dread of begging') deliberately answers the preceding chapter Iravu (ch. 106), which permitted asking only of fitting, generous givers; here Valluvar raises the ideal higher, so that even such givers should not be asked. Karavaadhu (கரவாது, 'without concealing') and uvandhu eeyum (உவந்தீயும், 'who give with delight') describe the best possible donor, and kannannaar (கண்ணன்னார், 'those like one's eyes') marks them as most precious; the hyperbole koadi urum ('attains a crore', i.e. ten-million-fold good) is the commentators' measure of the superiority of not asking. In the line of interpretation that follows Parimelazhagar, as reflected in Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan, the point is that dignity (maanam) lies in enduring want rather than in depending even on a willing friend. Pope renders it 'Ten million-fold 'tis greater gain, asking no alms to live, / Even from those, like eyes in worth, who nought concealing gladly give.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இரந்தும் உயிர்வாழ்தல் வேண்டின் பரந்து
கெடுக உலகியற்றி யான்.
transliteration:
Irandhum uyirvaazhdhal vendin parandhu
keduka ulagiyatri yaan.
current_meaning: If the maker of the world meant some people to live by begging, then let that maker also wander about like a beggar and die.
elementary: Imagine a game where the rules say some players must beg the others just to stay in. You would say the rules are unfair and the person who made them should try playing that way himself. That is how angry the Kural is that anyone should have to beg to live.
university: This is one of the boldest couplets in the Kural: Valluvar curses ulagiyatriyaan (உலகியற்றியான், 'he who fashioned the world') with the very fate of the beggar, parandhu keduga ('may he wander and perish'). Commentators in the tradition that follows Parimelazhagar read it as a conditional imprecation: if the creator had ordained begging as a means of life, he deserves to wander as beggars do; the force is ethical outrage that anyone should be reduced to irandhum ('even by begging') staying alive. Modern glosses differ in emphasis: Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the creator literal, while Kalaignar Karunanidhi's gloss pointedly says 'the one said to have created this world', distancing the verse from theism, and scholars have debated whether ulagiyatriyaan means a god, fate (ul), or the human order that permits destitution. Pope renders it 'If he that shaped the world desires that men should begging go, / Through life's long course, let him a wanderer be and perish so.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இன்மை இடும்பை இரந்துதீர் வாமென்னும்
வன்மையின் வன்பாட்ட தில்.
transliteration:
Inmai idumbai irandhudheer vaamennum
vanmaiyin vanpaatta thil.
current_meaning: There is no harder, more foolish idea than the bold thought that you can end the pain of being poor by begging instead of working.
elementary: If your bike breaks, you could keep asking friends to lend you theirs, or you could learn to fix your own. The Kural says choosing to ask forever instead of fixing things yourself is the worst choice of all.
university: The couplet plays on vanmai (வன்மை), 'hardness, toughness, boldness': the 'toughness' of deciding inmai idumbai (இன்மை இடும்பை, 'the affliction of want') will be ended by asking (irandhu theervaam) is called harder than any hardness (vanmaiyin vanpaattadhu il). Following Parimelazhagar's line, Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar supply the implied contrast with effort (muyarchi): the fault is abandoning work and choosing to live by others' gifts. Solomon Pappaiah adds the parenthesis '(without working it off)', and Pope's explanation speaks of remedying poverty 'by begging (rather than by working)'. Pope renders it 'Nothing is harder than the hardness that will say, / 'The plague of penury by asking alms we'll drive away'.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இடமெல்லாம் கொள்ளாத் தகைத்தே இடமில்லாக்
காலும் இரவொல்லாச் சால்பு.
transliteration:
Idamellaam kollaath thakaiththe idamillaak
kaalum iravollaach chaalbu.
current_meaning: A person who refuses to beg, even when they have nothing to live on, has a greatness so big that the whole world cannot hold it.
elementary: Think of someone who has almost nothing but still won't ask for handouts, because they want to stand on their own feet. The Kural says that kind of courage is so big that even the whole world isn't big enough to hold it.
university: The couplet turns on a pun on idam (இடம்): idamillaak kaalum means 'even when there is no means (of life)', while idamellaam kollaa means 'which all the room (of the world) cannot hold'. The quality praised is saalbu (சால்பு, 'nobility, fullness of character', the same root as saanraanmai, ch. 99), here specified as iravu ollaa, 'not consenting to beg'. In the line of commentary that follows Parimelazhagar, Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah take the second half as 'even when one is destitute' and the first as 'a greatness not equalled by all the worlds together'. Pope renders it 'Who ne'er consent to beg in utmost need, their worth / Has excellence of greatness that transcends the earth.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.
